records.title: Disparities in direct access to acute geriatric care – an observational analysis of geographic variations of ambulance conveyance
records.abstract: Ambulance services often represent a key entry point to healthcare for older adults, and subsequent care pathways have important implications for outcomes and resource use. Direct admission to geriatric units may offer benefits for certain patients, but access varies. This study aims to examine whether geographic area of residence is associated with ambulance conveyance to geriatric units as an alternative to emergency departments among older adults and to explore patient- and system-level factors associated with observed variation.  A cross-sectional, register-based study of ambulance assignments of adults ≥ 65 years in Stockholm, Sweden (2017–2019) was conducted. Eight geriatric units, each representing a distinct hospital service area, were included. The outcome was direct admission to a geriatric unit versus to an emergency department. Geographic variation was assessed using random intercept multilevel logistic models, adjusting for demand-side and supply-side factors, with measures of variation including intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), median odds ratio (MOR), and proportional change in variance (PCV).  Among 8208 patients included in the study, 603 (7%) were directly admitted to a geriatric unit. Crude conveyance rates across hospital service areas ranged from 4% to 21%. The unadjusted between-area variance (τ²) was 0.3510 (ICC = 0.096). When supply-side factors were assessed individually while controlling for demand, proximity to a geriatric unit, geriatric unit ownership, and number of staffed beds resulted in estimated reductions in the between-area variance by 26%, 27%, and 38%, respectively, suggesting that these factors may contribute to the observed area-level heterogeneity. In the fully adjusted model, τ² decreased by 41% to 0.2076 (ICC = 0.059), although considerable residual heterogeneity remained (MOR = 1.54), indicating that otherwise similar patients may face different probabilities of direct geriatric admission depending on their hospital service area. Robustness analysis with a Bayesian approach revealed large uncertainty around the estimated variance.  Direct ambulance conveyance to geriatric units varies substantially across hospital service areas. While proximity to units and greater geriatric bed capacity likely had an association with reduced between-area variation, meaningful residual differences persist, suggesting that unmeasured factors beyond patient need and measured supply characteristics may influence access to acute geriatric care.

records.title: Cigarette and e-cigarette tax effects on the oldest generation of smokers in the United States
records.abstract: and  As cigarette smoking continues to decline among youth and young adults, smoking rates among older U.S. adults remain unchanged. Historically, cigarette and, more recently, e-cigarette tax policies influenced smoking behavior in younger smokers. This study examined how older smokers respond to tax changes to inform public health strategies. Research Design and  Our data combined a panel of state cigarette and standardized e-cigarette tax rates with individual-level survey microdata. Our sample included adults aged ≥65, with and without a history of smoking. We estimated two-way fixed-effects population-weighted regression models of current smoking and past-year quit attempts. Exploratory subgroup analyses tested for heterogeneity by education and income level.  Among 3,117,382 adults, 48% had a history of smoking; of whom 18% currently smoked. A $1.00 cigarette tax increase was associated with current smoking: est. = -0.56 percentage points (pp) (CI: -0.85, -0.27). A $0.10 increase in e-cigarette tax (open) was associated with current smoking (+0.28 pp; CI: 0.01, 0.55). Approaching tax parity by one dollar was associated with a 0.48-pp (CI: 0.20, 0.76) increase in current smoking. While varied by socioeconomic status, there was no association between cigarette/e-cigarette taxes and quit attempts.  For older U.S. adults, cigarette taxes were associated with lower smoking, whereas e-cigarette taxes were associated with higher smoking. The type of e-cigarette tax appears important for tobacco control in older smokers. Policies increasing the relative cost of e-cigarettes may perpetuate smoking rates in older populations at the highest risk of smoking-related harm.

records.title: Feeling younger or older? How life events reshape subjective age among Chinese older adults
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Subjective age is a construct that displays considerable individual variability. This study, conducted within the Chinese context, investigates how major life events affect older adults’ subjective age, measured by felt age and look age, and the moderating effects of chronological age and community services for older adults.  We used a nationally representative sample of older adults aged 60 and over from three waves (collected in 2018, 2020, and 2023) of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey. Fixed-effects models were employed to examine how negative events (e.g., serious illness or death of a relative/friend) and positive events (e.g., a child’s marriage or childbearing) impact subjective age. Random-effects models were conducted for robustness checks.  The findings indicate that experiencing negative events is associated with an older subjective age by approximately 1.3% or 1 year. In contrast, witnessing positive events reduces their felt age and look age by roughly 0.9% or 0.6 years and 1.2% or 0.9 years, respectively. The negative impact of adverse events on subjective age intensifies with chronological age, whereas the rejuvenating effect of positive events attenuates. The availability of community services for older adults significantly reduces the impact of both negative and positive life events. Discussion The  highlight the complex relationship between life events and subjective age, suggesting that supportive environments can buffer older adults from the psychological effects of life transitions.

records.title: Race/ethnicity, completed parity, and women’s later-life health in the Health and Retirement Study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study examines associations between completed parity, including childlessness (zero parity), and a range of medical conditions (individually and cumulatively) and self-rated health, including differences associated with race/ethnicity-related factors.  We conduct correlational and multivariable regression analyses using a historical HRS/AHEAD sample of ever-married, non-Hispanic Black and White women born between 1920 and 1941. Multivariable models adjust for early-life-course social determinants of health, including contextual birthplace exposure to Jim Crow-era structural racial inequalities. We focus on childlessness/zero parity by using zero-inflated count regression  that statistically identify women with zero probability of having had a live birth (a latent “always-zero” group).  Black women had three times the odds of “always-zero” group membership and, if not in that group, an expected parity 11% higher than White women. In correlational analyses, the predicted probability of “always-zero” group membership (Predicted Infecundity Probability or PIP)—rather than reported childlessness status—and high parity were associated with high-fatality medical conditions and self-rated fair/poor health. In multivariable models, PIP and high parity were positively associated with number of conditions, while PIP and number of conditions were positively associated with self-rated fair/poor health. Net of parity, consistent with weathering, younger Black women had a higher-than-expected number of medical conditions relative to all women. Discussion In the context of historical structural racial inequality, race/ethnicity-related differences in childlessness and high parity were strongly associated with later-life, post-reproductive health disparities. Women’s number of births was associated with the accumulation of medical conditions in a U-shaped pattern.

records.title: Asymmetric behavioral responses to changes in subjective survival expectations: Implications for health investment in later life
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Subjective survival probability (SSP) is a key predictor of economic and health decisions in later life, yet existing research assumes that gains and losses in survival expectations have symmetric behavioral effects. This study examines how within-person changes in SSP are associated with health-promoting behaviors among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea.  Using ten waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2006-2024), we estimate individual fixed-effects models on an analytic sample of 65,069 person-wave observations from 10,878 individuals aged 45 and older. We extend the standard symmetric model by adopting an asymmetric fixed-effects framework, which decomposes cumulative SSP increases and decreases into separate parameters.  The symmetric model shows that a one-unit increase in SSP (on a 0-10 scale) is associated with a 0.69 percentage-point increase in regular exercise, after controlling for self-rated health, chronic diseases, functional limitations, and socioeconomic characteristics. The asymmetric decomposition reveals two distinct patterns: exercise responds exclusively to SSP losses (loss-only), while paid health checkups respond only to SSP gains (gain-only). Formal symmetry tests reject equal absolute effects for both outcomes (p Discussion These findings provide evidence that associations between changing survival expectations and health behaviors may be asymmetric. The domain-specific nature of these asymmetries—loss-only disengagement in exercise and gain-only investment in preventive care—suggests that interventions targeting middle-aged and older adults may benefit from considering potentially different mechanisms linking survival expectations to behavior across outcome domains.

records.title: Internalizing active aging norms: Self-attributed responsibility as a mediator linking prescriptive views on aging to late-life preparation
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
authors: M Clara P de Paula Couto
records.abstract: Older adults face prescriptive expectations about aging, including active aging norms emphasizing physical activity, social engagement, and autonomy. While previous research has linked active aging norms to health-related and social behaviors, no studies to date have examined whether and how these norms are related to proactive, future-oriented behaviors such as late-life preparation. Drawing on theories of norm internalization, this study examines self-attributed responsibility for aging preparation as a mediator linking active aging norms to late-life preparation.  Data were drawn from the Ageing as Future project and included 1,003 participants aged 34 to 90 years (M = 58.82 years; 52% female). Late-life preparation was assessed using two complementary indicators: a count-based checklist of concrete preparatory behaviors and a continuous scale of perceived preparatory engagement. Mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS models, with Poisson regression-based mediation applied to the behavioral count outcome.  Across both indicators, stronger endorsement of active aging norms was associated with greater engagement in late-life preparation. These associations were partially mediated by perceived responsibility, indicating that individuals endorsing active aging norms more strongly were more likely to perceive preparation as their own responsibility, which was itself associated with higher preparatory engagement. Discussion The findings suggest that active aging norms are associated with late-life preparation in part through a greater sense of personal obligation to manage one’s own aging process, highlighting the role of norm internalization and perceived responsibility in translating prescriptive views of aging into proactive behavior.

records.title: Family structure and transitions into and out of homeboundness: Evidence from the National Health and Aging Trends Study, 2011–2024
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Homebound status refers to needing assistance or an assistive device to leave home, being normally unable to leave home, or experiencing leaving home as a major effort. This study examines transitions into and out of homeboundness and whether family structure is associated with these transitions, with attention to gender differences.  Using National Health and Aging Trends Study data from 2011–2024, transition probabilities across four states—independent, homebound, nursing home residence, and deceased—were estimated using an unadjusted continuous-time homogeneous Markov model. Multinomial logistic regression models then assessed associations between family structure and subsequent transitions, including gender interactions.  Among respondents who were independent, 84.6% remained independent, and 12.2% became homebound by the next wave. Among those who were homebound, 23.6% returned to independence, 60.1% remained homebound, 2.4% entered nursing home residence, and 13.9% died. Unpartnered older adults had higher risks of transitioning from independence to nursing home (RRR = 1.752, p Discussion : Homeboundness as a dynamic and socially structured process. Family structure may shape pathways into homeboundness, institutional care, and death, with implications for aging in place.

records.title: Multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking behaviors among Latino older adults experiencing behavioral health problems
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: U.S.-based Latino older adult populations face disproportionate barriers to accessing behavioral health services. We examined associations between multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking from different sources of behavioral health supports among understudied Latino older adults with behavioral health problems.  Data come from a cross-sectional survey that included U.S.-based Latino residents ages 50-86 (N=274; 2021). The survey measured mental illness biopsychosocial causal beliefs, treatment efficacy beliefs, and social rejection beliefs as multiple facets of mental illness stigma that may influence mental and physical health help-seeking behaviors from four sources: traditional media, online/digital media, family/friends, and healthcare providers. Linear regression models examined associations between each stigma component and each help-seeking outcome, adjusting for personal/family factors in the full sample of Latino older adults and among a subsample reporting a self/familial behavioral health problem (n=173).  Among Latino older adults with self/familial behavioral health problems, higher biopsychosocial causal beliefs were associated with increased mental and physical health help-seeking from healthcare providers (p Discussion Multifaceted anti-stigma interventions for multi-generational Latino families may be an opportune strategy for increasing help-seeking for behavioral health problems among Latino older adults.

records.title: Rural and Urban Differences in the Trends in Supply of Home Care Workers From 2015 to 2024
records.abstract: Given the rapidly aging population in the United States and preferences to age-in-place, demand for direct care workers in the home will increase. Yet, it is unclear whether labor supply will meet demand, particularly in rural areas.  To describe differences in home care worker supply and demand by rurality and temporal trends between 2015 and 2024.  Repeated cross-sectional description of the supply of care workers serving adults 65 and older with functional impairments in the United States using 2015-2024 American Community Survey data.  From 2015 to 2024, the national supply of home care workers increased by 6.0% (95% CI: [2.6%, 9.4%]). Relative supply in metropolitan areas increased 7.3% (95% CI: [3.6%, 11.0%]) and decreased in rural areas by −10.3% (95% CI: [-19.7%, −1.0%]). While potential demand for care increased in both rural and metropolitan areas over this period, the number of care workers increased only in urban areas.

records.title: Sex-specific multimorbidity clusters and all-cause mortality among community-dwelling older adults: findings from the ASPREE cohort
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Multimorbidity is common in older adults, but sex differences in chronic condition clustering remain unclear. This study explored multimorbidity clusters and their associations with all-cause mortality among community-dwelling adults aged 70 years and over.  This was a secondary analysis of data from 16,095 Australian ASPREE participants aged ≥70 years without prior dementia or cardiovascular disease. Fifteen baseline chronic conditions were grouped using latent class analysis (LCA). Observed-to-expected (O/E) ratios characterized conditions over-represented within clusters, and Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations with all-cause mortality.  Among 16,095 participants (mean age 75.3 years), 88.3% had multimorbidity at baseline; 4,217 deaths occurred over a median follow-up of 10.85 years. Five clusters were identified overall: hypertension & dyslipidemia (52.1%), gout & metabolic (14.4%), depressive symptoms, osteoporosis & frailty (10.0%), anemia & kidney disease (10.2%), and hypotension, thyroid disorder & past cancer (13.3%). Sex-stratified analyses revealed three clusters in males and four in females. The frailty, depressive symptoms & osteoporosis cluster was associated with higher mortality in both sexes (aHR 1.56 [95% CI 1.40–1.73] in males; 1.68 [1.49–1.89] in females). Higher mortality was also observed for the metabolic, gout & kidney disease cluster in males (aHR 1.63 [1.47–1.81]) and the gout, anemia & kidney disease cluster in females (aHR 1.96 [1.74–2.21]).  Distinct multimorbidity clusters were identified overall and in sex-stratified analyses. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest the potential clinical utility of multimorbidity clusters to identify individuals at increased risk of death, but further research is needed.

records.title: Rethinking the Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Healthy Older Adults: The Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) Exergames
records.abstract: Though exergames attract considerable research interest as tools for preserving cognitive function in older adults, a decade of meta-analytic evidence reveals a persistent gap between theoretical promise and empirical demonstration: exergames rarely outperform conventional motor-cognitive training and do not generate the sustained engagement that preventive benefit requires. These  reflect limitations that are structural: the field focused predominantly on clinical populations rather than primary prevention; training concepts borrowed from rehabilitation protocols rather than grounded in the specific neuroplastic mechanisms of the exergaming medium; and virtual environments that are digitally sophisticated but culturally and esthetically neutral, systematically excluding the stimulation that converging evidence from neuroaesthetics, cultural epidemiology, and narrative neuroscience identifies as a core active ingredient of brain health promotion. To address these limitations simultaneously, this viewpoint introduces Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) exergames, defined as “virtual reality solutions in which motor-cognitive interactions are embedded in artistic content, cultural heritage, or historically situated narrative to exploit optimal neurobiological substrates of the intervention.” Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework, we develop mutually reinforcing mechanistic pillars: multimodal sensorimotor engagement within ecologically valid immersive environments; semantic and narrative activation of memory systems; emotional and autobiographical resonance as a dopaminergic driver of learning consolidation and sustained participation; and the re-engineering of physical effort evaluation from aversive to appetitive through aesthetic pleasure and narrative absorption. A fundamental implication is that in MAGIC exergames, motivation is not engineered through gamification mechanics—it is released by the intrinsic value of inhabiting a culturally meaningful world. We further argue MAGIC exergames correspond to a specific use that is, Cultural Snacking, which consists of the serialization of MAGIC content into brief, narratively open daily episodes of 5 to 10 minutes, designed for 3 to 5 daily consumptions across varied contexts. This dosing architecture is compatible with the motivational profile of healthy older adults who do not identify as patients or trainees. The paper opens perspectives with a design and research agenda structured around three priorities: characterizing MAGIC exergames by the type of motor-cognitive interactions they deliver rather than by the technology platform; conducting mechanistic neuroimaging investigations targeting the specific biomarkers of neuroplastic benefit that creative cultural engagement is expected to produce; and building the intersectoral innovation ecosystem that brings cultural institutions, digital health teams, and older adults together as co-designers. Without waiting for MAGIC-specific trials, we invite the digital medicine, public health, and silver economy communities to recognize that museums, heritage sites, and cultural institutions are potentially the most ecologically valid, intrinsically motivating, and cost-effective substrates for a new generation of brain health exergames that are as meaningful as they are effective. The scientific, institutional, and economic conditions for this convergence already exist.

records.title: Knowledge Performance, User Experience, and Cybersickness With Immersive Virtual Reality for Tai Chi Movement-Encoding in Older Adults: Randomized Comparison Study
records.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used for embodied training, but its practical value for older adults depends on whether the experiential benefits can be achieved without unacceptable discomfort or overstated claims about motor learning.  This randomized study compared head-mounted immersive VR with standardized, content-matched 2D video instruction for Tai Chi movement-encoding in community-dwelling older adults.  A total of 106 older adults were randomized to immersive VR (n=56) or video instruction (n=50). The primary analysis included 92 participants with complete age, pretest, and posttest data (VR: n=45; Video: n=47). The primary outcome was a 5-item movement-encoding knowledge score (range 0‐20), analyzed using analysis of covariance, with posttest score as the dependent variable and group, pretest score, and age as predictors. Secondary outcomes were intrinsic motivation, game experience, and learning engagement; safety, tolerability, and feasibility were assessed using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, Game Experience Questionnaire, Utrecht Work Engagement Scale–Short Form, participant flow, and Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire. VR system telemetry was analyzed descriptively as an exploratory process outcome.  Adjusted posttest movement-encoding performance did not differ between VR and video instruction (adjusted difference −0.27, 95% CI −2.25 to 1.72; P =.79; partial η 2 =0.001). The Game Experience Questionnaire  favored VR for competence (Video: mean 3.36, SD 1.21; VR: mean 4.15, SD 0.92; q =0.009), flow (Video: mean 3.77, SD 1.26; VR: mean 4.46, SD 0.76; q =0.014), and lower tension (Video: mean 1.76, SD 1.04; VR: mean 1.27, SD 0.63; q =0.037), whereas challenge did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction ( q =0.073). In the VR Group, recognition accuracy was associated with posttest movement-encoding score (n=44; r =0.317, P =.04), but pose accuracy was not (n=44; r =0.129, P =.41). The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire scores were low among valid VR participants (total score mean 3.77, SD 11.12), and 36 out of 46 (78%) participants reported zero symptoms.  With a strong active control, immersive VR did not produce higher short-term Tai Chi movement-encoding performance than video instruction. Among participants who completed the VR session, the immediate game-experience profile was more favorable. These findings indicate that VR may offer experiential benefits, while also highlighting the need to manage cybersickness and technical exclusions and to distinguish movement knowledge from actual motor execution.

records.title: Social Determinants and Oral Health Among Indigenous and Non-Indigenous Older Adults in La Araucanía, Chile: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: Social disparities in oral health persist, disproportionately affecting Indigenous populations.  This study aims to compare oral health status, dental care access, treatment needs, and social determinants between Mapuche and non-Mapuche older adults in the La Araucanía Region of Chile, within a hybrid dental care model, and to explore whether ethnicity is associated with these outcomes, guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH) framework.  We conducted a cross-sectional exploratory analytic study using data from 480 adults aged 60 years or older who received dental care through a hybrid teledentistry and mobile clinic model (Geriatric Dental Specialties Tele-Platform [TEGO]) in 4 municipalities of La Araucanía. The analytic sample was restricted to community-dwelling, functionally independent older adults. Outcomes included oral health status (nonfunctional dentition, edentulism, cavitated caries, and periodontitis), dental care access (fixed prosthetic rehabilitation and unmet denture need), and dental treatment needs (restorative and prosthetic). Structural (sex, age, education, rurality, and ethnicity) and intermediary determinants (behavioral, biological, psychosocial, and health system access) were analyzed following the WHO-CSDH framework. Bivariate analyses compared outcomes between Mapuche and non-Mapuche participants. Multivariable logistic regression models examined associations between determinants and outcomes.  A total of 471 older adults (mean age 72.8, SD 7.7 years) were included; 76.9% (362/471) had nonfunctional dentition, 18% (85/471) were edentulous, 25.6% (98/383) had cavitated caries, and 46% (154/335) had periodontitis. In bivariate analyses, Mapuche participants showed lower educational attainment, higher rural residence, poorer oral health, more behavioral risk factors (eg, infrequent toothbrushing and higher sugar intake), greater restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care compared with non-Indigenous peers. In multivariable analyses, female sex was associated with increased odds of edentulism but lower odds of periodontitis. Lower education was associated with nonfunctional dentition (odds ratio [OR] 4.28, 95% CI 2.34-7.88; P  Oral health inequalities among older adults in La Araucanía were associated with both structural and behavioral determinants. Although Mapuche participants exhibited poorer oral health, higher restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care in bivariate analyses, ethnicity remained associated only with cavitated caries and periodontitis in adjusted models. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating social determinants into oral health planning for underserved older adults and highlight the potential utility of data generated through digitally supported territorial care models for informing equity-oriented oral health strategies.

records.title: Clinical and Geriatric Profiles of Centenarians Living in Long-Term Care Facilities in Martinique, a Validated Blue Zone, and Neighboring Guadeloupe (French Caribbean Islands)
records.abstract: Martinique has recently been described as one of the world’s five “Blue Zones” of longevity, while the status of Guadeloupe remains to be established. This study described the observed proportion and clinical and geriatric profiles of centenarians living in sampled long-term care settings in Martinique and Guadeloupe. Data from two observational cohorts of nursing home ( n = 332) and foster family residents ( n = 107) were pooled. Among 439 participants, 13 (3.0%) were centenarians (mean age 102.1 ± 2.4 years; 76.9% women). Compared with younger residents (mean age 80.8 ± 9.8 years), centenarians had similar prevalences of major comorbidities and polypharmacy, but greater functional impairment and poorer physical performance. One-year mortality was higher among centenarians (58.3% vs. 21.4%; p = 0.002). In long-term care settings, exceptional longevity was characterized by greater functional impairment and mortality without a greater burden of major chronic diseases.

records.abstract: Informal caregivers of people with dementia experience substantial psychological burden, affecting caregiver well-being and care sustainability. records.title: The relationship between health literacy and active and successful aging: a cross-sectional study of active aging service center
records.abstract: While successful aging focuses on physical health and disease prevention, active aging offers a broader framework encompassing social participation and security. Health literacy is considered a vital tool in achieving these outcomes, yet its specific impact on the synergy between both aging paradigms requires further exploration.  This study aims to evaluate the relationship between health literacy, successful ageing, and active ageing among older adults and to identify the factors associated with active ageing levels. Method This descriptive and cross-sectional study was conducted between October 2024 and May 2025 at the Metropolitan Municipality’s Active Aging Service Center in Antalya, Türkiye. The study included 306 participants aged 65 and over. Data were collected using a Demographic Information Form, the Active Ageing Scale, the Successful Ageing Scale, and the Turkish Health Literacy Scale. Data analysis included descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, Chi-square, Pearson correlation, and Multiple Linear Regression.  The study involved 306 older adults with an average age of 67.79 ± 3.56 years (79.4% of participants were women, and 70.6% were university graduates). Whilst the majority of participants reported having a chronic illness (66.0%) and taking medication regularly (64.7%), 58.5% engaged in regular physical exercise and 80.7% engaged in regular mental activities. The mean total score for the Active Ageing Scale was 190.10 ± 39.37, for the Successful Ageing Scale it was 57.74 ± 7.61, and for the Health Literacy Index it was 32.97 ± 9.53. Bivariate analyses revealed that higher levels of education, income, regular physical exercise and mental activity were significantly associated with better health literacy and ageing outcomes ( p p p  Health literacy is a key factor of active and successful ageing. To promote active ageing, older adults care centres should prioritise health literacy.

records.title: Positioning Care Robots Within Filial Responsibility: Perspectives of Chinese Only Children
records.abstract: The adoption of care robots for older adult care is often framed as a question of whether older adults will accept the technology. This paper argues that, in family-based care for older adults at home, an equally important question is how adult children position care robots within intergenerational care relationships and their responsibility for ageing parents. Using Q methodology with 42 Chinese only children, by-person factor analysis identified four profiles: the Worried Controller, who may prioritise safety over parental autonomy; the Modern Filial, who sees tailored robots as a contemporary expression of filial piety; the Presence Keeper, who resists technologies that substitute for family presence; and the Filial Complementarity Conditionalist, who sees robots as supplementary to filial and emphasises broader policy and service conditions. These profiles show how participants balance filial obligation, caregiving pressure, parental autonomy, family presence, and wider conditions surrounding care-robot use.

records.title: Social Capital and Life Satisfaction Among Older Adults in South Korea: The Role of AI Literacy
records.abstract: Bonding (close, homogeneous ties) and bridging (weaker, heterogeneous ties) social capital are associated with older adults’ life satisfaction, but the indirect role of AI literacy remains unclear.  To examine direct and indirect associations among bonding and bridging social capital, AI literacy, and life satisfaction among Korean older adults.  Data from 1,250 adults aged ≥65 years in the 2024 Digital Divide Survey were analyzed using structural equation modeling and 5,000 bootstrap resamples.  Both social capital forms and AI literacy were positively associated with life satisfaction. Bridging social capital was positively associated with AI literacy, whereas bonding social capital was negatively associated. Their indirect associations were 0.063 (95% CI 0.040–0.090, P Discussion Bonding and bridging ties may shape older adults’ AI learning differently, suggesting that social context matters for AI literacy and life satisfaction.

records.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with heat-related illness in a super-aged society: a cross-sectional study of older adults in suburban Tokyo, Japan
records.abstract: The convergence of increasing extreme heat events due to climate change and rapid population aging poses a critical public health challenge. While previous studies have identified risk factors for heat-related health outcomes, most have been conducted in Western countries and have relied on indicators that require resource-intensive surveys. This study aims to identify factors associated with heat-related illness among the elderly in Japan using practical, policy-relevant indicators.  A cross-sectional study using a self-administered questionnaire was conducted in a suburban area of Tokyo, Japan, from September to November 2017. Elderly residents were recruited from two distinct populations: a large public housing complex and a socially active community club. The primary outcome was the self-reported history of heat-related illness within five years, defined as episodes requiring ambulance transport or hospital visits. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors (Significance level: p  Of the 743 participants included in the analysis (mean age: 73.01, SD: 10.23), 31 (4.17%, 95% CI: 2.86%–5.87%) reported having experienced heat-related illness. In the univariate analysis ( p N = 583), factors that remained associated with heat-related illness ( p  Advanced age and living alone were strongly associated with heat-related illness, while air conditioning ownership was inversely associated. Utilizing easily accessible administrative data—such as age, household composition, and long-term care status—is a feasible strategy to identify vulnerable older adults and target proactive interventions in super-aged societies.

records.title: The impact of population aging on household carbon emissions and its heterogeneity: evidence from CGSS 2018 data in China
records.abstract: Against the backdrop of the “Dual Carbon” goals and accelerated population aging, changes in household demographic structure may influence household carbon emissions; however, existing research has not fully examined these effects and their heterogeneity at the micro household level. This study aims to investigate the impact of population aging on household carbon emissions and its heterogeneity based on Chinese household microdata.  Using data from the 2018 China General Social Survey (CGSS), this study employed the STIRPAT model and OLS regression. It characterizes population aging from three dimensions—“whether there are elderly members”, “proportion of elderly members”, and “average age of elderly members”—to examine its impact on total household carbon emissions, direct carbon emissions, and indirect carbon emissions, and further analyzes the heterogeneity of urban-rural, regional, climate conditions, as well as the mediating effect of household expenditure.  This study found a significant negative correlation between population aging and household carbon emissions, with the “structural effect” being stronger than the “age effect”. Households with elderly members have significantly reduced carbon emissions, and the higher the proportion of elderly members, the more significant the reduction in household carbon emissions. The impact of population aging on indirect carbon emissions is stronger than that on direct carbon emissions, indicating that it mainly exerts its effect by reducing expenditure and adjusting consumption structure. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the reduction in household carbon emissions caused by population aging is more pronounced in rural, central, and northern China.  Population aging has reduced household carbon emissions, which is of significant value for low-carbon governance. Policymakers should incorporate population aging into the household emission reduction framework and consider urban-rural and regional differences to promote differentiated low-carbon policy design.

records.title: Impact of family video calls on depression and perceived social support among older adults residing in nursing home residents in Tabriz
records.abstract: Introduction Elderly people may need to stay in nursing home for various reasons. Separation from family may affect depression and perceived social support in older adults. This study aimed to investigate the effect of video communication on depression and perceived social support in nursing home residents.  This quasi-experimental study was conducted in 2022 on 61 older adults in nursing homes in Tabriz, Iran, using cluster sampling. Participants were randomly assigned to intervention ( n = 29) and control ( n = 32) groups. The intervention group received weekly video calls with family over two months alongside routine visits; while the Control group received routine visits only. Depression and perceived social support were assessed at baseline and after two months using Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 ( p  After the intervention, the mean depression score in intervention group was significantly lower than control group (Effect size = 0.87, p = 0.001). The mean perceived social support score (Effect size = 0.67) in the intervention group was significantly higher compared to the control (Effect size = 0.67, p = 0.01).  Video calls with family were associated with reduced depressive symptoms and increased perceived social support among nursing home residents. These findings show that video communication can be used in nursing homes to enhance the short-term well-being of residents.

records.title: Worried, deterred, and still interested: Psychological barriers and older adults’ intentions to adopt smart home technologies
records.abstract: and  Smart home technologies (SHTs) hold promise for supporting aging in place, yet older adults’ technology adoption involves more than a straightforward response to perceived benefits. This study examined how privacy concerns and fear of dependency, along with other technology acceptance factors, are associated with behavioral intention to use SHTs, and whether these associations differ between older adults with and without prior SHT experience. Research Design and  We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of 421 U.S. older adults aged 55 to 80. Drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, we assessed performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, along with privacy concerns and fear of dependency. Multiple regression analyses with interaction terms were estimated separately for experienced and inexperienced users, and pooled models with three-way interactions tested whether moderating associations differed by prior experience.  Performance expectancy predicted intention across both groups, while fear of dependency was negatively associated with intention. Privacy concerns strengthened the relationship between social influence and intention, and fear of dependency strengthened the relationship between performance expectancy and intention among experienced users. The moderating association of privacy concerns did not differ significantly by experience, whereas the moderating association of fear of dependency did.  Concerns about privacy and dependency were associated with the conditions under which older adults found SHTs compelling, suggesting that endorsement from trusted others and clear evidence of functional benefit may matter most for those who hold such concerns.

records.title: Range and Consistency of Reported Outcomes in Interventional Studies involving Frail Inpatients: A Systematic Review
records.abstract: and  Many interventions have been developed to improve outcomes for frail inpatients. No reviews have comprehensively mapped out these outcomes. This paper aims to assess the range and consistency of outcomes reported in interventional studies involving frail adult inpatients and identify whether the outcomes were patient-reported. Research Design and  A systematic review of interventional studies involving frail adult inpatients from 2000 to 2026 was conducted, using the following databases: MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). All reported outcomes were extracted and catalogued to assess reporting range and consistency.  From 74 included studies, 545 outcomes were identified and categorised into 43 domains. Among 545 outcomes, physical performance was the most frequently reported domain (n = 69, 12.7%), followed by mortality/survival (n = 43, 7.9%) and quality of life (QoL) (n = 36, 6.6%). Of the 74 included studies, mortality/survival was reported in 33 studies (44.6%), followed by physical performance (n = 27; 36.5%), and QoL (n = 26; 35.1%). Nearly half of the domains (44.2%) were measured in only one to three studies, including those directly related to the hospital experience. Of the 545 outcomes, 141 (25.9%) were classified as patient-reported outcomes.  There was heterogeneity and inconsistency in outcomes reported across interventional studies involving frail inpatients. This limits comparability and synthesis of study findings. The development of a core outcome set informed by the priorities of patients and caregivers, alongside healthcare professionals, would enhance the consistency, relevance, and quality of frailty research and better support patient-centred care.

records.title: Hallmarks of Aging Associate with High Intensity Interval Training Benefits and Frailty in Female C57Bl/6J Mice
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Frailty and cognitive decline are common among older adults, increasing risks of disability and loss of independence. We have previously demonstrated in mice that short session (≤10 minute) high-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an effective intervention for frailty, but benefits for cognitive function and reducing hallmarks of aging have not been examined. Thus, we studied 24-month-old female C57BL/6J mice from our previous study that remained sedentary or performed a 10-minute HIIT regimen 3-days-a-week for 8 weeks. We found HIIT improved cognitive aspects including an increase in T-maze alternation % and novel object recognition, but no differences were observed in Barnes maze or light-dark preference. To explore HIIT impacts on the hallmarks of aging, we examined liver, gastrocnemius muscle, and cortex brain tissues for mitochondria expression, autophagy, cellular senescence, and telomere length. HIIT increased expression of mitochondrial complexes I and V, as well as PGC1α and SIRT3 in all tissues. Autophagy marker beclin was elevated across all tissues, while p62 was increased in liver and muscle but not in the cortex, and LC3-II was lower in muscle and liver. Senescence marker p16 was lower in HIIT muscle and liver, whereas p21 decreased in liver but increased in muscle. Telomere lengths were greater in liver, but no changes in muscle or cortex. Additionally, within the group of sedentary mice, we identified differences in hallmarks of aging that potentially underlie frailty as measured using different mouse frailty assessment tools. These  highlight the potential for multi-tissue geroprotective benefits of short session HIIT to reduce frailty and improve cognition for healthy aging.

records.title: Alda-1 Alleviates the Cognitive Deficits in D-galactose-induced Aging Mice by Regulating Oxidative Stress, Neuroinflammation, and Mitochondrial Biogenesis
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Although mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) is involved in aging and age-related neurodegenerative diseases, the impact of ALDH2 on age-related cognitive deficits and its underlying mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to explore the effects of ALDH2 on cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice and illustrate the potential molecular mechanisms. We treated D-galactose-induced aging mice with Alda-1 (a potent agonist of ALDH2) for eight weeks and observed the alterations in behavior, levels of oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related genes. The  revealed that Alda-1 alleviated neuropathological changes in the hippocampus and ameliorated cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice. Administration of Alda-1 further reduced the levels of 4-HNE, MDA, 3-NT, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β; enhanced Mn-SOD and CAT activities; increased GSH and ATP levels and mitochondrial content; and upregulated PGC-1α/NRF-1/TFAM expression in the hippocampus of D-galactose-induced aging mice. Moreover, in D-galactose-treated HT22 cells, we found that the SIRT1 inhibitor EX527 reversed the Alda-1-induced upregulation of PGC-1α, suggesting that the Alda-1-induced upregulation of PGC-1α is associated with SIRT1 signaling. Collectively, Alda-1 ameliorated cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice by reducing neuroinflammation, enhancing antioxidative capability, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, and modulating the SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling pathway.

records.title: Experiences from a language development intervention in nursing homes from the perspective of first-line managers, language advocates and care staff: a qualitative study
records.abstract: An increase in foreign-born workers in nursing homes (NHs) has challenged first-line managers to implement language initiatives for their staff. Evidence regarding foreign-born care workers’ experiences of language support initiatives is still scarce. Thus, the aim of the study was to explore and describe the experiences of a language development intervention “Talk about Work” from the perspective of first-line managers (FLMs), language advocates and participating care staff.  An explorative qualitative study using on-going evaluation  following the intervention “Talk about Work.” The intervention consisted of eight workshops intended to strengthen language and professional competence within health and social care. Semi-structured focus-group interviews were conducted with FLMs (3), language advocates (5), and caring staff including language assistants (20) at NHs. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify three main categories and seven subcategories.  The educational material was suitable for caring staff, and FLMs found it beneficial also for future education plans. They could repeat topics, introduce new ones, and continue the intervention at different paces. Addressing Swedish language skills at work was perceived as sensitive, and the initiative made it easier to speak about language competences. Challenges for FLMs included finding staff with the right competences to lead the initiative. Language advocates asked for closer collaboration with FLMs.  The intervention “Talk about Work” was considered appropriate for and was well received by all participating groups in the study. Moreover, FLMs could use the material for continued language initiatives at NHs. To improve language and communication skills among caring staff in multi-cultural contexts, there is a need to find staff with the right competences to lead language development initiatives as well as to provide resources to implement them.

records.title: Prediction of 2-Year Incident Clinical Knee Osteoarthritis From Extensor Mechanism Mechanical Properties in Asymptomatic Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Prospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) lacks disease-modifying treatment, making early identification of modifiable risk factors in asymptomatic older adults a priority. Patellar tendon stiffness (PTS) and knee extensor strength (KESt) may independently influence KOA development, yet their prognostic value in individuals free of knee symptoms is unestablished.  This study aimed to determine whether baseline extensor mechanism mechanical properties predict 2-year incident clinical KOA in community-dwelling older adults who were asymptomatic at enrollment, and to quantify the relative contribution of each parameter.  This 2-year prospective cohort study enrolled 116 community-dwelling older adults (220 knees) free of knee pain at baseline. Incident clinical KOA was diagnosed according to the American College of Rheumatology criteria. Prognostic performance was evaluated across 7 survival algorithms using 5-fold nested cross-validation with the Harrell C-index. Predictor importance was quantified using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values from the best-performing model, and absolute KOA risk was estimated across tertiles of the linear predictor score.  Over 2 years, 55 (25%) knees developed incident clinical KOA. PTS and KESt were consistently selected across all cross-validation folds, whereas quadriceps muscle passive stiffness was not selected in any fold. The gradient boosted survival model achieved the highest discrimination (C-index=0.720, 95% CI 0.686-0.754), significantly exceeding chance ( P  PTS and KESt independently and consistently predicted 2-year incident clinical KOA in asymptomatic community-dwelling older adults. Extensor mechanism mechanical profiling may identify individuals at elevated KOA risk prior to symptom onset, although these exploratory findings require confirmation in larger cohorts before KESt and PTS can be considered for screening or preventive intervention.

records.title: Participatory Approaches with Older Adults in Technology and Innovation Research: A Scoping Review of Reviews
records.abstract: Compared to other age groups, older adults are often marginalized in the design processes of digital technologies leading to digital and social exclusion. While these aspects have been discussed in several reviews, an overarching perspective on how older adults are involved in Participatory Approaches (PA) in technology and innovation development is currently missing. This scoping review of reviews provides an overarching view on the narratives, trends, and gaps in PA in different fields of innovation, and proposes future research and practice directions. The study followed the Arksey & O’Malley’s protocol for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR checklist as the reporting guideline. Seven databases were screened for studies with a thematic focus on older adults, applying PA in technology and technology-related innovation, and published between 2014-2024. Twenty-two reviews were included. PA with older adults have seemingly evolved over the years with an increased focus on values equity, empowerment, power-sharing, and mutual learning. Nevertheless, deficit narratives on aging and ageism still constrain meaningful participation. A "participation gap" persists in which: terminology remains inconsistent; older adults are predominantly assigned roles of informants or testers rather than co-designers or equal partners;  are mainly data-extractive; marginalized subgroups remain systematically underrepresented; and the technology scope remains predominantly care-centric. Identified gaps highlight the need for standardizing meaningful participation by creating a seal of quality for participatory approaches, improved reporting, and stronger inclusion of underrepresented populations and life domains of older persons.

records.title: Digital Reminiscence-Based Interventions to Enhance Social Interaction of People With Dementia in Care Homes: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: The use of digital tools in reminiscence interventions has increased in recent years, encompassing multimedia platforms, virtual reality (VR), digital life storybooks, and interactive applications. Yet, evidence regarding the effectiveness of digital reminiscence-based interventions remains limited. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesise the existing evidence on digital reminiscence-based interventions in care homes, with a focus on: (i) their development and evaluation; (ii) the extent to which they address cultural diversity and inclusivity; (iii) the support provided to end users; and (iv) the barriers and facilitators influencing their implementation. A systematic search of five databases (MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science), and three grey literature sources (BASE, King’s Fund Database, PsyArXiv) was undertaken. Reference lists of key papers were also hand-searched. Studies of all methodologies (qualitative, quantitative, and mixed ) were included. Sixteen studies involving 365 participants met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were grouped into: (i) digital reminiscence, (ii) digital life story, and (iii) immersive VR. Reminiscence and life story interventions improved emotional wellbeing and social engagement, while VR mainly supported stimulation and mood. Stakeholder involvement in design of technology was limited, especially for people with dementia, and reporting on cultural diversity was minimal. Variation in intervention design and outcomes limited  on overall effectiveness. Implementation facilitators were ability to personalise content, care provider/home manager support, staff engagement and training, and family involvement. Barriers included technology usability, organisational infrastructure and support, workforce knowledge and capacity, and difficulties integrating into routine care practices. Digital reminiscence generally improved wellbeing, mood, cognition, communication, social interaction, although findings were mixed and limited by small samples, and varied intervention designs and outcome measures. Future research should prioritise co-creation with people with dementia, families, and staff; include more diverse populations across the disease trajectory; and explore sustainable integration into routine care practice.

records.title: Appropriateness prescriptions of direct oral anticoagulants in hospital in 2023 in the older population: a prospective observational multicenter study
records.abstract: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed, particularly in outpatient settings by general practitioners. In older patients with polypharmacy, inappropriate DOAC prescribing represents a major patient safety concern, potentially leading to therapeutic failure or preventable harm. To assess the quality and safety of DOAC prescriptions at hospital admission and discharge among older adults in 2023. Secondary  were to identify factors associated with inappropriate prescribing, characterize underlying prescribing errors, and compare these findings with data from 2018.  We conducted a prospective, observational, multicentre study across three French university hospitals, including departments of cardiology, internal medicine, post-emergency, and acute geriatrics. Older adults who were taking DOACs prior to admission and hospitalized for >24 hours were consecutively enrolled between November 2022 and May 2023. Appropriateness was defined according to European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines. Predictive factors were analyzed using logistic regression, and comparisons with 2018 data were made using χ² tests.  Of 536 eligible patients (mean age 84.1± 8.5 years; 50.6% women), 421 were included in the primary analysis. Most received apixaban (70.1%) for atrial fibrillation (83.6%). Inappropriate prescriptions were identified in 32.0% on admission and 24.9% at discharge (p = 0.004). Age >80 years (OR=1.80, CI95%= 1.20-2.72) and serum creatinine >133 µmol/L (OR=1.84, CI95%= 1.13-2.98) were associated with admission inappropriateness; age >80 years remained a discharge risk factor (OR=2.71, CI95%= 1.63-4.61), while weight  Inappropriate DOAC prescribing during hospital transitions remains common in older adults, driven by advanced age and impaired renal function. The absence of substantial improvement since 2018 suggests that further efforts to optimize DOAC prescribing are warranted. Future interventions, including pharmacist-led medication reviews and integrated prescribing tools, could be considered to improve DOAC prescribing appropriateness in older adults. Trial registration Clinical trial not applicable.

records.title: Healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning related to mealtimes in long-term care facilities: an interview study
records.abstract: Mealtimes in long-term care facilities are complex and serve multiple purposes. They provide opportunities for participation and learning, involving residents, relatives and healthcare professionals, each with unique circumstances. Participation and learning are central to healthy ageing. Healthcare professionals play a key role in enabling participation and learning among those involved, although these opportunities may be shaped by their perceptions and attitudes. Therefore, this study aimed to explore healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning among residents, their relatives, and colleagues related to mealtime situations in long-term care facilities.  Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews with 23 healthcare professionals (nursing assistants, licensed practical nurses, and registered nurses) working in long-term care facilities in a municipality in south-eastern Sweden. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.  Three themes were generated: (1) Shaped by relationships and circumstances , (2) Rewarding yet challenging , and (3) Prerequisites influence opportunities. Participation and learning related to mealtime situations manifested in various ways and to differing degrees, from extensive to almost non-existent. It was a balancing act for the healthcare professionals managing multiple challenges to enable participating and learning; however, residents and relatives were seldom invited to engage in this problem-solving. For participation and learning to occur, prerequisites were required at all levels in the organisation.  Healthcare professionals perceive that participation and learning among residents, relatives, and colleagues in long-term care facilities do occur, but to varying degrees and are associated with multiple challenges. Drawing on a learning model, such as Illeris, can help identify which components need to be developed, which together with a deeper understanding and implementation of person-centredness, could contribute to increased participation and learning, and thereby to the wellbeing of residents, relatives, and healthcare professionals. However, this approach must permeate the entire organisation.

records.title: Racial-Ethnic Differences in Healthcare Experience Among Middle-Aged and Older Adults in the United States: Evidence From Four Waves of the Health and Retirement Study
records.abstract: Racial and ethnic inequities in U.S. healthcare extend beyond insurance and access, yet less is known about how they vary across domains of healthcare experience and whether public insurance mitigates these inequities.  Using four waves (2014–2020) of Health and Retirement Study data ( n = 16,088), this study examines disparities in satisfaction, affordability, accessibility, and preference concordance among middle-aged and older adults.   show domain-specific disparities: Black, Hispanic, and “Other” respondents had higher odds of unmet healthcare preferences than non-Hispanic White respondents, while affordability gaps persisted. Differences in overall satisfaction were largely attenuated after adjustment, whereas Black respondents reported fewer accessibility barriers. Medicaid mitigated some disparities, particularly for Hispanic respondents in affordability and preference concordance, whereas Medicare showed limited moderating effects, with gains in satisfaction being more evident among non-Hispanic White respondents. Discussion Overall, inequities persist beyond socioeconomic and health differences, highlighting structural and interpersonal factors in shaping healthcare experiences.

records.title: Physical Performance and Daytime Sleepiness as Correlates of Life-Space Mobility in Community-Dwelling Older Adults
records.abstract: Life-space mobility reflects the extent and independence with which older adults move within their environments and is an integrative indicator of functional capacity and social participation.  To examine associations of physical performance and daytime sleepiness with life-space mobility among community-dwelling older adults.  A cross-sectional study was conducted among 403 older adults in Chile. Life-space mobility was assessed using the Life-Space Assessment (LSA), physical performance with the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and daytime sleepiness with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Pearson correlations and multivariable linear regression were used to evaluate associations adjusting for age and sex.  Better physical performance and lower daytime sleepiness were associated with greater life-space mobility in bivariate analyses. In adjusted models, physical performance remained associated, whereas daytime sleepiness was not.  Physical performance is an important correlate of life-space mobility and may serve as an indicator of functional vulnerability in older adults.

records.title: The Shift to Social Care Contracting Between Health Care Entities and Community-Based Organizations
records.abstract: Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) play a critical role in coordinating health-related social services such as nutrition and medical transportation for older adults in their communities, yet their formal engagement with health care entities varies widely. This study examines organizational characteristics of AAAs associated with their shift to contracting with health care organizations. The study analyzed data using repeated waves of the National Survey of AAAs and the Community-Based Organization-Health Care Contracting Survey. Logistic regression assessed how organizational characteristics are associated with contract formation. Findings reveal that shifting into formal contracting was more likely for independent non-profit AAAs, those AAAs that provided care transition services, and AAAs with high annual budgets. Higher proportion of funding received from the Older Americans Act was negatively associated with a change in contracting status. This study suggests that organizational autonomy, financial stability, and diverse funding streams are associated with a higher capacity for entering into health care contracts.

records.title: The direct medical cost of urinary and fecal incontinence by care settings for adults over 65 in the United States
records.abstract: Incontinence is a chronic condition that affects millions of adults over the age of 65 in the United States. This study estimates the direct medical costs of incontinence for this population and identifies some possible root causes driving these costs.  This retrospective analysis relied on administrative claims data from the 2018 Medicare Limited Data Set. The cost analysis was limited to fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare beneficiaries over the age of 65 enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B. Our analysis of urinary tract infections (UTIs) relied on a Medicare Advantage dataset from 2016 to 2018 that included service and drug costs. We used diagnosis codes and place-of-service codes from the 2018 claims experience to identify incontinent members and their respective care setting. We used propensity score matching of incontinent and non-incontinent members to estimate the incremental cost of incontinence, controlling for age, gender, regional state groupings, and 79 comorbidities based on ICD-10CM codes, categorized into 9 disease groups. We also created an event study of UTIs to explore whether the cost of a UTI episode differs based on the presence of incontinence.  On average, direct medical costs for incontinent members were $404 per member per month (PMPM) in 2018 USD higher than their non-incontinent counterparts in the same care setting. This gap rises to $968 PMPM when averaged over all members across all four care settings because it accounts for the disproportionate migration of incontinent members into more intensive and expensive care settings. A significant driver of these costs is the higher prevalence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) among incontinent members. Using an event study of UTIs, we also find that the treatment costs for UTIs are 52% higher, on average, for incontinent members.  The direct medical cost of incontinence for adults over 65 is comparable in magnitude to other major chronic conditions such as obesity, cancer, and diabetes, yet receives far less policy and management attention. Payers and institutions can make meaningful gains in reducing this cost by investing in incontinence management strategies that reduce UTIs, support caregivers, and prevent transitions to higher-intensity care settings.

records.title: Service use after long-term care entry: low utilization and early dropout in Taiwan
records.abstract: and  Home- and community-based services (HCBS) are central to Taiwan’s long-term care (LTC) system, yet some users show limited service use after entering the system. This study examined predictors of two patterns of limited HCBS use: low utilization and early dropout. Research Design and  This study analyzed administrative LTC records from Pingtung County, Taiwan, among cases entering the LTC system during 2019–2021: 17,517 in the low-utilization analysis and 18,678 in the early-dropout analysis. Low utilization was defined as service use in the lowest quartile of service-use days per 30 follow-up days, and early dropout as case closure within 90 days. Bootstrap-enhanced least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (BoLASSO) was applied, followed by multivariable logistic regression.  Low utilization was associated with care arrangements and entry pathways, including institutional residence, use of a paid migrant caregiver, co-residence with a nonfamily caregiver, and entry via the 1966 hotline. Early dropout occurred in 11.4% of cases and was associated with cancer, oxygen-related care needs, severe pain, underweight, unintentional weight loss, and inability to complete short-term memory assessment. Service-provider referral was associated with lower odds of both outcomes.  Low utilization and early dropout showed distinct predictor patterns: the former was more closely associated with care resources and entry pathways, whereas the latter was associated with health instability and recent decline. Distinguishing these patterns may inform more tailored care management and service delivery based on users’ needs and care contexts.

records.title: Understanding the Benefits of Textiles in Facilitating Interactions for People With Dementia: An Exploration of Design Considerations and Recommendations
records.abstract: As the global population of people with dementia increases, the demand for best practice dementia care is growing. Textiles have the potential to assist with interacting with people with dementia and provide benefits in dementia care settings. However, there is currently limited understanding of, or experience with, the specific challenges, considerations and design of interactive textile products for people with moderate to advanced dementia. This exploratory qualitative study aimed to explore the perspectives of using interactive textiles with people with dementia. Seven sets of interactive textiles were tested for usability with nine people with dementia, followed by post-testing interviews. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with care partners and healthcare professionals to understand the effects of interactive textiles in two care settings. In total, 27 people were interviewed, including people with dementia ( n = 9), informal care partners ( n = 5), formal care partners/staff ( n = 2), and healthcare professionals ( n = 11), from a residential care home, a daycare centre, and a university located in southeastern Australia. The findings highlighted several benefits of interactive textiles, including assisting interactions, facilitating communication, providing sensory stimulation, supporting reminiscence, and promoting positive emotions such as reducing stress and anxiety. Participants suggest textiles can be used to provide engagement, describing the importance of forging connections between people with dementia and their past, bolstering familiar associations, emotional relations, and recognition of personal preferences. These insights informed design considerations and recommendations for creating interactive textiles that offer playful and meaningful activities for people with dementia.

records.title: Feasibility of the DIGNITY Intervention to Support Person-Centered Risk Management  in Rural Nursing Homes
records.abstract: Honoring individual preferences, like going outside, can enhance the health of nursing home (NH) residents living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Although a hallmark of person-centered care, honoring ADRD residents’ preferences is often restricted when they are perceived to be high-risk for harm by NH staff. Accessible and efficient strategies are needed to help NH staff balance harmful risks to health and safety against the residents’ right to make autonomous choices, especially in under-resourced rural areas. This pilot study (NCT05618678) evaluated the feasibility of Decision-making In aGing and demeNtIa for auTonomY (DIGNITY), a multi-faceted and innovative, theory-based, person-centered risk management intervention aimed at assisting NH staff in respecting the preferences of rural residents living with ADRD, while optimizing safety. Feasibility was assessed using retention rates, staff surveys, and qualitative feedback. Fifty-two NH staff participated (88.7% female, 83.3% White, 94.3% non-Hispanic, and 48% with ≥6 years NH experience), with a 79% retention rate and 87.8% survey response rate. In the DIGNITY group, average scores (on Likert scale of 1–5) indicated high feasibility (3.99), acceptability (4.19), and appropriateness (4.24). Qualitative feedback highlighted the value of in-person training and telemonitoring sessions. The high ratings for feasibility, acceptability, and appropriateness of DIGNITY show its potential for supporting NH staff to more confidently provide person-centered care for ADRD residents.

records.title: Life-Course Adversity, Adult Socioeconomic Position, and Possible Sarcopenia Among Older Adults in Postwar Vietnam
records.abstract: This study examines how early-life hardship, wartime exposure, military service, and adult socioeconomic position are associated with grip strength–based possible sarcopenia among older adults in postwar Vietnam.  We analyzed data from the Wave 1 Vietnam Health and Aging Study among 2,166 adults aged 59 and older. Possible sarcopenia was defined using Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia 2019 grip-strength thresholds; survey-adjusted logistic regression models were used.  Possible sarcopenia prevalence was 46.86%. Childhood hunger and poor childhood health showed limited associations; wartime stress exposure and military service were not significant in fully adjusted models. Lower odds were associated with higher household assets (OR = 0.91), secondary education or higher (OR = 0.56), professional occupations (OR = 0.60), and other non-agricultural occupations (OR = 0.70).  Possible sarcopenia in Vietnam reflects not only age-related muscle decline but also the social patterning of later-life vulnerability through adult socioeconomic resources.

records.title: Acceptance of AI-Based Assistive Technologies for Autonomy Support Among Older Adults: A Scoping Review
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Population aging is leading to increased demand for health and long-term care. AI-based assistive technologies have been developed to support autonomy and care for older adults, yet real‑world adoption remains limited. We review evidence on acceptance and determinants of acceptance of AI‑based assistive technologies among older adults.  We conducted a scoping review using the JBI methodology and followed PRISMA‑ScR guidelines for reporting. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane) were searched for studies published from January 2010 to June 2025, initially in any language. We included studies examining acceptance and determinants of acceptance of AI-based assistive technologies among adults aged 65 years and older. We synthesized data using inductive thematic analysis.  Twenty‑nine studies met the inclusion criteria, with over one-third conducted in Europe (n = 10). Overall attitudes toward AI‑based assistive technologies were generally favorable when technologies were perceived as useful, easy to use, and tailored to needs. However, actual use was low. Acceptance was associated with socio‑demographic (e.g., age, residence), medical (e.g., frailty, self‑rated health), psychosocial (e.g., stigma), and structural (e.g., cost, accessibility) determinants, as well as with institutional and relational factors (e.g., preservation of human contact).  While older adults have generally positive views of AI‑based assistive technologies, adoption is slow because of intersecting psychosocial, economic, technical, and organizational barriers. User‑centered design, care-led innovation approaches, and implementation strategies that complement—rather than replace—human support may facilitate uptake and sustained use. Development of standardized assessment tools is needed to enable cross-study comparability and guide future research.

records.title: Correlates of Subjective Cognitive Impairment Among Community Dwelling Older Non-Hispanic Black and Non-Hispanic White Men
records.abstract: Subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) predicts Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Identifying SCI correlates may identify cognitive risk earlier in the ADRD continuum. We examined SCI correlates among older non-Hispanic Black (NHB) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) men. Method Cross-sectional data were from 669 men in the 2012 National Health and Aging Trends Study. Logistic regression was used to identify SCI correlates, accounting for complex sampling and attrition. Result Higher education (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.13–0.87) and former smoking (OR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.16–0.91) were associated with lower SCI odds. Sleep difficulties (OR = 2.81, 95% CI: 1.22–6.47), multimorbidity (OR = 2.16, 95% CI: 1.09–4.29), and ADL disability (OR = 4.19, 95% CI: 2.03–8.61) were associated with higher odds. Discussion Education, smoking status, sleep, multimorbidity, and functional status may be important SCI correlates among older NHB and NHW men. Addressing modifiable correlates may support cognitive health earlier in the ADRD continuum.

records.title: Is there a role for artificial intelligence in end-of-life care for persons with dementia? Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff
records.abstract: and  Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families’ and staff’s acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia. Design and  In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.  Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants’ narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.  Families and frontline staff should not be considered merely as end users, but as key stakeholders whose needs and expertise should shape the direction of AI applications.
