records.title: Purpose in Life Among Older Adults: A Machine Learning Analysis of Potential Predictors
records.abstract: A sense of purpose is a central component of mental well-being in older adulthood. Although many predictors of purpose have been identified, most studies have considered a limited set, leaving their relative importance unclear. The present study addressed this gap by examining a large set of psychological, social, and demographic variables in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults from the Health and Retirement Study. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was used to evaluate 47 predictors. Self-esteem emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by positive affect. The leading predictors were organized into six domains: adaptive self-related beliefs, affective well-being, perceived control, optimism, social engagement, and spirituality/religiosity. Demographic variables were less predictive overall. These findings indicate that individual differences in purpose are associated with a broad set of psychological resources involving self-regulation, interpersonal processes, optimism, and positive affect.

records.title: Performance of Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-For-Service Populations
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse (CCW) algorithms are widely used to identify chronic conditions in Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) claims. However, their validity in Medicare Advantage (MA) encounters remains uncertain.  We conducted a cross-sectional study using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare data. We analyzed NHATS Rounds 9 and 11, aged≥65 years, with continuous 24-month enrollment in MA or FFS. CCW algorithms were applied to identify six conditions: arthritis, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, and osteoporosis. Self-reported, physician-diagnosed conditions from NHATS interviews served as the reference standard. Survey-weighted sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and balanced accuracy were compared between MA and FFS.  We included 1,708 MA and 2,239 FFS beneficiaries in Round 9 and 1,472 MA and 1,566 FFS beneficiaries in Round 11. Across both rounds, balanced accuracy was similar between MA and FFS for all six conditions. Diabetes and hypertension demonstrated high sensitivity (0.88–0.94), while arthritis and osteoporosis showed lower sensitivity but high specificity. Although statistically significant MA–FFS differences were observed for select metrics (diabetes PPV in Round 9; chronic lung disease specificity in Round 11), absolute differences were minor and not clinically meaningful.  CCW algorithms perform comparably in MA and FFS Medicare data. These findings support the validity of using CCW algorithms in MA encounter data for epidemiologic research for risk adjustment, facilitating more generalizable studies of the growing MA population.

records.title: Performance of Claims-based Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Evidence comparing the performance of claims-based dementia algorithms across Medicare Advantage (MA) and fee-for-service (FFS) populations remains limited. We evaluated the validity of two claims-based algorithms across MA and FFS populations.  We used nationally representative, linked National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS)-Medicare data to identify community-dwelling participants with continuous enrollment in MA or FFS during Round 7 (2017; n = 5,018), Round 9 (2019; n = 4,018), and Round 11 (2021-2022; n = 3,086). Using NHATS probable dementia as reference standard, we validated the Bynum-Standard and Chronic Condition Warehouse (CCW) dementia algorithms across three time points.  Overall, both algorithms demonstrated comparable performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity (>97.9%) and negative predictive value [NPV] (>92.9%). The Bynum algorithm showed similar sensitivity between MA and FFS in Rounds 7 (30.2% vs. 29.1%) and 11 (25.6% vs. 23.9%), but lower sensitivity in MA for Round 9 (25.0% vs. 36.4%). Positive predictive value [PPV] was similar between MA (62.7%-70.6%) and FFS (62.1%-70.4%) across all rounds. The CCW algorithm demonstrated greater MA-FFS differences, with lower sensitivity in MA for Rounds 9 (30.8% vs. 46.9%) and 11 (35.0% vs. 49.3%) and similar sensitivity for Round 7 (40.4% vs. 42.2%). PPV varied across rounds in both MA and FFS [(Round 7: 76.3% vs. 71.2%) to (Round 11: 68.5% vs. 76.4%)]. Both algorithms identified participants with more severe dementia.  Claims-based dementia algorithms demonstrate broadly consistent performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity and moderate PPV but comparable or lower sensitivity in MA, informing case ascertainment across Medicare plan type.

records.title: Performance of Claims-based Frailty Indices in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Despite growing enrollment in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, the performance of claims-based frailty algorithms, which were developed for Medicare fee-for-service (FFS), remains unclear in MA.  We calculated the Kim claims-based frailty index (CFI), Veterans Affairs-Frailty Index (VA-FI), and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) and MA data. We evaluated their performance against the comprehensive geriatric assessment-based frailty index (CGA-FI) and the frailty phenotype (FP) in Round 11 and Round 9.  Among 1,527 FFS and 1,457 MA beneficiaries in Round 11, frailty prevalence was 34.2% and 35.5%, respectively, by CGA-FI ≥0.25, and 13.3% and 16.2%, respectively, by FP. Across FFS and MA populations, the CFI, which prioritizes specificity and positive predictive value, classified 10-12% of the overall population and 30-36% of those with prior hospitalization as frail, whereas the VA-FI and HFRS, which emphasize sensitivity, classified 53-71% of the overall population and 56-87% of those with prior hospitalization as frail. Although claims-based frailty measures performed similarly across FFS and MA populations, their discriminatory ability was higher for CGA-FI ≥0.25 (C-statistics: CFI, 0.79-0.82; VA-FI, 0.77-0.82; HFRS, 0.63-0.77) than for FP (CFI, 0.71-0.77; VA-FI, 0.67-0.75; HFRS, 0.60-0.74). Performance was consistent by race and survey rounds, with modestly better discrimination in women than men.  Claims-based frailty measures are scalable tools for contemporary FFS and MA populations. However applying published thresholds led to differences in frailty prevalence and model performances. Thresholds should therefore be tailored to the intended.

records.title: Dental Coverage and Dental Care Utilization Among Medicare Advantage Beneficiaries With and Without Diabetes United States
records.abstract: To examine dental visits, dental coverage, and out-of-pocket (OOP) dental expenditures among Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollees with and without diabetes.  We analyzed 2015–2019 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey data for MA enrollees aged ≥65 years ( N = 12,312). Outcomes included any dental visit, any OOP expenditure, and total OOP spending among those with positive expenditures. Multivariable regression models examined associations between diabetes, dental coverage, and utilization outcomes.  Diabetes was associated with lower odds of having a dental visit (AOR = 0.84), whereas dental coverage was associated with higher odds of dental visits (AOR = 1.85) and zero OOP expenditures (AOR = 3.36). No significant interaction effects were observed between diabetes and dental coverage.  Dental coverage alone may be insufficient to improve dental care utilization among adults with diabetes. Integrating oral health into chronic disease management may improve dental utilization among older adults with diabetes.

records.title: Life Course Neighborhood Socioeconomic Disadvantage and Chronic Disease Accumulation in Mid- to Late Adulthood
records.abstract: This study examines associations between neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage during adolescence and early adulthood and chronic disease accumulation in mid- to late life.  Using Panel Study of Income Dynamics data linked to U.S. Census and American Community Survey data, we identify four trajectories of neighborhood disadvantage, namely persistent disadvantage, increasing disadvantage, decreasing disadvantage, and persistent advantage, and estimate their associations with chronic and cardiometabolic conditions diagnosed between ages 40 and 75.  Compared with persistent neighborhood advantage, persistent and increasing disadvantage are associated with chronic disease burden, net of individual and contemporaneous neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. Associations between decreasing disadvantage and multimorbidity are largely attenuated after adjustment for individual socioeconomic characteristics.  Persistent neighborhood disadvantage is associated with greater chronic disease accumulation, while worsening disadvantage is particularly associated with cardiometabolic burden, highlighting the relevance of earlier-life inequality for aging. Adolescence and early adulthood may represent sensitive periods, with early adulthood potentially more consequential for chronic disease burden.

records.title: Social Isolation, Loneliness, and Cognitive Decline Among Black Americans: The Moderating Role of Neighborhood Context
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Our study examined how social disconnection, neighborhood contexts, and cognitive function trajectories are jointly and interactively associated among middle-aged and older Black adults.  Data came from non-Hispanic Black participants aged 51 and older (n = 1,791) from the Health and Retirement Study. Cognitive health was measured by a global cognitive function summary score. Social disconnectedness was measured by three types of social isolation (from extended family, adult children, and friends) and loneliness (UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale). Neighborhood contextual factors included neighborhood social cohesion and physical disadvantage. Covariables included age, sex, education, marital status, and living arrangements. We used group-based trajectory modeling to test the study .  We identified four global cognitive function trajectories: low and declining (14% of sample), moderate and declining (29%), moderate and stable (40%), and high and stable (17%). Multivariable models indicated that neighborhood physical disadvantage (RRR=.61, 95%CI[0.40, 0.92]) and social cohesion (RRR=.42, 95%CI[0.23, .77]) moderated the association between social isolation from extended family and global cognitive function trajectory membership.  Our study is among the first to examine cognitive function trajectories with linkages to social disconnectedness and neighborhood contexts among middle-aged and older Black adults. Overall, the  suggest that neighborhood contexts condition how social isolation relates to cognitive trajectories. These findings underscore the importance of considering both social disconnectedness and neighborhood context in explaining heterogeneity in cognitive aging among middle-aged and older Black adults.

records.title: DNA methylation variability provides a complementary epigenetic signature of aging heterogeneity: Findings from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Human aging does not follow a single trajectory. Epigenetic changes offer insight into the heterogeneity in aging by reflecting the combined influence of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors on the timing and progression of age-related changes beyond what chronological age alone can explain. Recent studies in cancer and aging underscore the importance of methylation variability as a marker of biological dysregulation.  We investigated the role of DNA methylation in aging heterogeneity by performing epigenome-wide differential methylation and variance association analyses in blood samples from 1,445 Canadians aged 45 to 85 from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging.  We identified 448 differentially methylated regions and 488 differentially variable regions associated with health decline as measured by the health deficit accumulation Frailty Index, cognitive function, and physical function. These two classes of regions showed minimal overlap, with distinct gene coverage, suggesting that variability contributes a complementary signal to aging heterogeneity. Genes overlapped by differentially methylated regions were enriched for immune and inflammation-related pathways, whereas differentially variable regions highlighted additional localized, CpG‑island–enriched signals shared across health domains, consistent with regionally structured rather than diffuse dysregulation. By integrating significant CpGs from both analyses, we constructed an epigenetic biomarker. The biomarker was associated with all-cause mortality and showed higher discrimination than biomarkers constructed from differential methylation or variability alone, with a similar pattern reproduced in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.  These findings suggest that DNA methylation variability may provide a complementary dimension of epigenetic aging and support further evaluation in larger cohorts with more mortality events.

records.title: Development and Temporal External Validation of a Parsimonious, Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting 6-Month Mortality in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Retrospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Early mortality after long-term care facility (LTCF) admission is common; yet, prognostic tools are often derived from Western minimum dataset-based cohorts or require hospital electronic health record linkages that are unavailable at intake in many LTCFs. There is also limited evidence on explainable, admission-feasible machine learning–based prognostication in Asian LTCF settings.  The aim of the study is to develop and temporally externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting 6-month all-cause mortality among older adults newly admitted to LTCFs in Taiwan using routinely collected LTCF assessment data.  We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the JUBO Long-Term Care Database, a nationwide private administrative registry covering 636 LTCFs (37.4% of the national LTCFs) in Taiwan. We included residents with first-time LTCF admission and prespecified nonoverlapping cohorts for temporal validation: development (January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2023; n=23,901) and external validation (January 1 to December 31, 2024; n=6216). The outcome measure was death within 180 days of admission. We compared a nonlinear ensemble model (hybrid of extreme gradient boosting and random forest [HybridXGBRF]) with 7 other algorithms, including tree-based and linear benchmarks. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, and F 1 ), and calibration (Brier score and calibration plots) were assessed. Model interpretability was examined using Shapley Additive Explanations.  In the development cohort, 5272 of 23,901 (22.1%) residents died within 180 days. In the 2024 temporal validation cohort, 1781 of 6216 (28.7%) residents died. In internal cross-validation, HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models (0.89, 95% CI 0.88‐0.89). In temporal validation, HybridXGBRF maintained strong discrimination (AUROC 0.90, 95% CI 0.89‐0.91), with an accuracy of 0.85 and an F 1 -score of 0.68. Calibration plots indicated close agreement between predicted and observed risks across most probability ranges, with mild divergences at higher predicted risks. Shapley Additive Explanations analysis identified frequent hospitalizations within 6 months, activities of daily living impairment, and weight loss as influential predictors. The model showed stable AUROC across sex and age strata (0.89‐0.90) and maintained high discrimination among residents with improving activities of daily living scores (AUROC 0.91, 95% CI 0.90‐0.92).  An interpretable machine learning model using routinely collected Taiwanese LTCF assessment data achieved strong discrimination, acceptable calibration, and stable temporal validation performance without requiring hospital-based electronic health record linkage. The HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models, but performance differences from extreme gradient boosting were small. The model may serve as a risk-stratification tool to help identify residents who could benefit from structured care review, advance care planning, or palliative care assessment. Prospective implementation studies could determine its impact on care processes and resident- or family-centered outcomes.

records.title: Conditional pathways to loneliness in older adults with vision impairment: A decision-tree analysis
records.abstract: and  The prevalence of vision impairment continues to increase globally due to population growth and aging. Among older adults with vision impairment, loneliness is common. Prior studies assessing loneliness risk have relied on regression-based approaches, which may not capture complex, heterogeneous conditional pathways. We apply a theoretically guided machine learning approach to examine loneliness risk among older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Research Design and  Using baseline data from 210 adults with AMD (Agemean = 80.1 years) enrolled in a randomized controlled trial, we applied a decision tree method using measures of legal blindness, emotional responses to vision loss, social life satisfaction, anxiety, depression, optimism, future planning, and sociodemographic factors to investigate heterogeneous pathways to loneliness.  Decision tree models demonstrated stable discrimination (AUCtrain=.88, AUCtest=.78, DeLong 95% CI: 0.68–0.88) and robust classification performance across thresholds. Social life satisfaction emerged as the primary branching condition differentiating loneliness outcomes. Distinct pathways suggested that high social life satisfaction was strongly associated with lower loneliness; optimism served as a compensatory resource when social satisfaction was lower. Additional pathways highlighted the effects of vision loss severity, anxiety, and emotional responses to vision loss on loneliness. Depressive symptoms differentiated loneliness outcomes within a lower-anxiety branch, suggesting depression may overshadow protective factors.  These findings suggest that loneliness arises through heterogeneous psychological pathways rather than single risk factors. By identifying conditional configurations of psychosocial and health-related factors, interpretable decision-tree models may inform more targeted screening, evaluation, and intervention strategies.

records.title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Nursing Home Staffing Gaps Relative to the 2024 U.S. Federal Minimum Staffing Standards
records.abstract: The 2024 U.S. federal minimum staffing rule for nursing homes was vacated and repealed before taking effect, but states continue to adopt their own standards. Whether uniform standards impose uneven compliance burdens is unclear.  To examine whether the 2024 federal minimums differed by neighborhood deprivation.  Cross-sectional analysis of 9,315 U.S. nursing homes linking CMS-reported staffing (April to June 2025) with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI).  Overall, 42.8%, 67.0%, and 31.3% of facilities staffed below the registered nurse (RN), nurse aide, and total nursing minimums, respectively. Facilities in the most deprived tercile staffed 0.103 RN hours per resident day lower than the least deprived (95% CI, −0.161 to −0.045), with 2.28 times the odds of falling below the RN minimum.  Uniform staffing standards would concentrate compliance burden on facilities serving deprived urban communities. Future state or federal standards should pair minimums with financing and workforce supports.

records.title: Oral Health Indicators as Important Predictors of Frailty in Korean Adults Aged 50 Years and Older: A Sex-Stratified Explainable Machine Learning Approach
records.abstract: Frailty is a major public health concern, yet oral health indicators are rarely incorporated into prediction models.  To develop sex-stratified explainable machine-learning models for frailty prediction.  Cross-sectional data from 12,302 adults aged ≥50 years (KNHANES 2016–2019) were analyzed. Frailty was defined using a modified Fried phenotype, with robust and prefrail participants combined as non-frail. Five algorithms were developed separately for men and women and evaluated on independent test sets. Top-performing models were interpreted using SHAP.  The survey-weighted frailty prevalence was 14.1% (95% CI, 13.3–14.9). Test-set AUROCs ranged from 0.73 to 0.78 in men and 0.75 to 0.81 in women. XGBoost was selected for interpretation. Chewing and speaking difficulties ranked above hypertension in both sexes. Chewing difficulty showed complementary support in removal analyses. Smoking status and toothbrushing after meals ranked more prominently in men, whereas unmet dental care need and mouthwash use ranked more prominently in women.

records.title: “Someone’s Acknowledged My Mum…in that Moment she Connected”: A Qualitative Study of Family Benefits of Elder Clowning for Persons With Dementia in Long-Term Care
records.abstract: Elder clowning is a multi-component, person-centred intervention delivered to persons living with dementia in long-term care to enhance quality of life through individualised social engagement. Although persons with dementia are the target recipients of the intervention, their families may also derive benefits. However, their perspectives currently remain unexplored. This study aimed to explore whether and in what ways families of persons living with dementia in long-term care benefit from elder clowning interventions, from the perspectives of families and long-term care staff. Semi-structured interviews with family members of persons living with dementia and long-term care staff were conducted in four long-term care homes in Eastern Australia. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed according to Braun and Clarke’s Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Analysis of family member ( n = 11) and staff ( n = 20) perspectives on elder clowning generated two main themes: (1) transforming the emotional experience of visiting and (2) strengthening family connections through the shared experience. Elder clowning supported families to have improved visiting experiences with their relative in long-term care, which eased visit-related stress before, during, and after visits. Person-centred engagement through elder clowning was perceived to support the reciprocal interaction and happiness of their relative, which supported positive emotions for families. Families learned about their relative’s communicative capacity and new dementia-specific communication skills, which they then implemented independently from elder clowning. Shared positive experiences supported socialisation, reminiscence, and memory-making, which may have supported family connections. Elder clowning also provided families with opportunities for social support. While some families were actively involved, others preferred to watch, and some were perceived to decline involvement. Families expressed preferences or suggestions regarding intervention delivery, such as continuity and access. The benefits of elder clowning were found to extend beyond entertainment to support psychosocial wellbeing of families of persons living with dementia in long-term care.

records.title: Longitudinal Trajectories of Hospitalizations in U.S. Older Adults with Heart Failure
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Little is known about long-term risks of hospitalizations among heart failure (HF) older adults at a national level. We identified long-term patterns of hospitalizations following the diagnosis of HF and assessed whether high-risk patients can be identified prior to discharge.  This is a retrospective cohort study from 2010 to 2020. Fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF during an inpatient stay and followed for up to 5 years. Group-based trajectory models (GBTM) identified 4 trajectories of all-cause hospitalizations during follow-up. LASSO regression was used to identify patients’ baseline characteristics to predict their hospitalization trajectories. Model discrimination was assessed using C-statistics and calibration was evaluated using expected-to-observed ratios.  Of the 84,597 Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF (mean age: 77.4 [± 7.1] years and 58.3% male), we identified 4 distinct trajectories of hospitalizations: Group 1 (n = 19,340; 22.9%) had consistently “low risks” of hospitalization, Group 2 (n = 53,922; 57.9%) had elevated risks shortly after discharge (“high-to-low risk”), Group 3 (n = 5,035; 9.8%) had elevated risks at later stages of illness (“low-to-high risk”), and Group 4 (n = 6,300; 9.4%) had consistently “high risks” of hospitalization. Models were well-calibrated predicting hospitalization trajectories (compared to low-risk patients [Group 1]), and C-statistics were 0.65 (Group 2), 0.68 (Group 3), and 0.79 (Group 4). Discrimination was consistently better among patients ≤70 years and calibration remained excellent across all subgroups with expected-to-observed ratios near 1.0.  High-risk HF patients could be identified at the time-of-diagnosis using routinely available clinical characteristics, enabling targeted interventions during critical periods to improve long-term outcomes.

records.title: WHO-ICOPE–Aligned Multidomain Interventions for Intrinsic Capacity in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials
records.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) reflects older adults’ physical and mental abilities, and its decline predicts loss of independence. The WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) framework promotes multidomain, person-centred interventions, but evidence from trials remains limited.  To synthesise findings from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating WHO-ICOPE–aligned interventions in community-dwelling older adults.  Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (PROSPERO CRD420250654375), five English-language RCTs published from January 2020 to December 2025 were included. Participants had decline in at least one IC domain. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and findings were narratively synthesised due to heterogeneity.  One trial implemented the full ICOPE pathway; four used partial approaches. Improvements were most consistent for locomotion and vitality, while cognitive and psychological findings varied and sensory effects were generally limited. No consistent advantage of full over partial implementation was established.  Evidence remains limited and heterogeneous; further high-quality trials are required.

records.title: Aging-Related Diseases in the U.S. Population: A Data-Driven Approach Using All of Us Electronic Health Record Data
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Aging is the strongest risk factor for most chronic diseases, yet aging-related diseases (ARDs) lack consistent, data-driven definitions. Prior work has proposed frameworks to classify ARDs based on age-specific onset patterns, but applications have largely relied on demographically homogeneous populations.  We extended a data-driven framework integrating unsupervised clustering and actuarial modeling to electronic health record data from 633,547 participants in the U.S. All of Us Research Program. Age-specific onset rates for 274 high-burden diseases between ages 21 and 74 were analyzed. Standardized onset curves were grouped using hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Aging-related patterns were assessed with Gompertz and Gompertz-Makeham (GM) models to quantify age-dependent increases in disease onset.  Eleven clusters of disease onset trajectories were identified, with four main clusters encompassing 96.0% of diseases. Two clusters exhibited pronounced late-life increases in onset rate, while one showed earlier but moderate age-related increases, and another displayed largely age-independent patterns. Cardiovascular diseases and cancers were enriched in clusters with strong aging-related onset trajectories. Overall, 165 diseases demonstrated strong evidence of being aging-related, characterized by positive Gompertz age coefficients and good GM model fit. Median onset ages varied across clusters and disease categories and showed statistically significant discrepancies compared with U.K. populations.  In a large, racially diverse U.S. cohort, we identified distinct ARD clusters with shared age-related onset patterns. These findings extend prior work to a more diverse population and support integrated clustering and actuarial approaches to systematically define ARDs and inform aging research and public health strategies.

records.title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.  Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.  Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).  WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.

records.title: Exploring the Role of Race and Ethnicity in Resident-to-Resident Aggression: A Qualitative Study
records.abstract: and  Resident-to-resident aggression (RRA) is the most common form of elder mistreatment in long-term care settings. Although race/ethnicity is likely a contributing factor, research has been limited in examining the role of residents’ race and ethnicity in RRA. We sought to define and qualitatively examine the predisposing factors and acute precipitants of race/ethnicity-related resident-to-resident aggression (RE-RRA). Research Design and  Guided by the socioecological model, events-based perspective, and conceptual work on stigma-based aggression, we developed qualitative interview and data analytical guides. We conducted nine focus groups and twelve in-depth interviews with 81 nursing home staff from multiple clinical and non-clinical roles across two long-term care facilities on the U.S. East Coast. We coded qualitative data using a deductive thematic qualitative approach.  RE-RRA appeared to be a recurring interpersonal dynamic, though its full scope is likely under-detected and under-recognized. We identified five major types of RE-RRA, including physical violence, microaggression, social exclusion, and avoidance. Ten predisposing factors and eight acute precipitants uniquely contributed to RE-RRA, highlighting the importance of considering distinct race- and ethnicity-related elements in prevention research. We summarized our findings in a conceptual framework for RE-RRA that may be useful for future research.  RE-RRA is a distinct phenomenon shaped by identifiable predisposing and precipitating factors, offering opportunities for future prevention and intervention development. These findings underscore the importance of integrating RE-RRA within staff education, existing clinical governance structures, including incident reporting, and quality improvement processes.

records.title: Identifying Palliative Care Consultation Outcomes in Nursing Homes: Insights from Key Partners
records.abstract: and  Palliative care (PC) consultation outcomes in nursing homes (NHs) are often assessed using health systems' clinical and utilization metrics rather than outcomes from the perspective of the key partners who provide and sustain it. This study was designed to identify meaningful PC consultation outcomes from the perspectives of NH staff, PC consultants, and NH/PC agency directors. Research Design and  Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the team conducted semi-structured interviews with key partners from 14 NHs in the Eastern United States. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using conventional content analysis.  Participants (N = 33) included NH staff (e.g., primary care providers and nurses), PC consultants (e.g., PC physicians and PC nurse practitioners), and leaders (e.g., NH directors and PC agency directors). Key partners reported meaningful outcomes in four domains: resident, family, NH staff, and NH facility. Resident outcomes included goal-concordant care, symptom management, hospitalization rates, and understanding of care choices and control. Family outcomes included shared decision-making, understanding of the resident’s disease trajectory and management measures, and feeling supported. NH staff outcomes included capacity to provide high-quality care and emotional support. Lastly, NH facility outcomes included filling care gaps, facility reputation, and organizational morale.  These findings highlight multi-domain and interdependent PC consultation outcomes across residents, families, staff, and NH facilities that may be overlooked in existing evaluation frameworks. Future interventions and quality measures should incorporate these outcomes and ensure that residents’ and families’ perspectives are represented.

records.title: Living History, Fading Minds: Dementia as the Gateway to Historical Past in South Africa via Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019)
records.abstract: This manuscript analyzes the literary, social and cultural representations of dementia in Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019). I contend that the authors’ accounts of their mothers’ struggle with dementia, from its onset to its end, function as living archives of personal and national history. I employ life writing, aging studies, and, to a lesser extent, historiography to examine the literary, social cultural, and historical dimensions of such experiences. I address the narrative construction of the mothers’ identity in later life by highlighting the role of archives and family memories in the context of contemporary South Africa. Thus, I aim to illustrate the instrumental role of life narratives in the creation of safe spaces for intergenerational dialogue and reconciliation with a troubled past on a personal and national level. I also contend that humanities-based inquiry brings to the fore the essential aspects of later life, thereby challenging the pathologizing medical in the representation of dementia, which often disregards the reality of old people as vessels of knowledge. Eventually, I showcase that illness life narratives function as accessible repositories of public knowledge that render visible the realities of aging.

records.title: Cognitive reserve and everyday functioning in cognitively unimpaired older adults: evidence from the CAN-PROTECT study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Cognitive reserve (CR) is thought to buffer against the clinical manifestation of dementia, preserving cognitive function despite accumulating pathology. However, less is known about how CR relates to the capacity to independently perform activities of daily living (ADL), particularly among cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults. Here, we investigated this association.  Baseline data from 1,571 CU participants (mean age: 64.7±7.6; 81.3% female) from the CAN-PROTECT study were analyzed. A composite CR score was derived from education, occupational complexity, and engagement in cognitively stimulating activities. Functional ability was measured using the Standard Assessment of Global Everyday Activities (SAGEA) scale, capturing cognitive, applied cognitive, instrumental, and basic ADL, and mobility. Negative binomial models examined associations between CR and global and domain-specific ADL, adjusting for age, sex, cognition, behaviour, and physical/sensory limitations. Additional models tested the independent contribution of CR components to functional outcomes. Mediation analyses assessed the effect of CR on quality of life (QoL) through ADL abilities.  Higher CR was associated with lower global ADL impairment (count ratio=0.58, 95%CI: 0.36-0.94, p = 0.027), driven by 49% less impairment in applied cognitive ADL (95%CI: 0.26-0.97, p = 0.038). Among CR domains, education showed the most consistent association with lower impairment across all ADL domains and was indirectly linked to better QoL through improved function.  CR, particularly education, may play an important role in supporting functional abilities and QoL among CU older adults. Enhancing CR may be a promising avenue to promote functional independence and healthy aging, even in the absence of cognitive impairment.

records.title: Where the Wildfires Are: Correlates of Disaster Preparedness Among Oregon Assisted Living Communities
records.abstract: Assisted living communities (ALs) serve a growing population of older adults with long-term care needs, especially those with Alzheimer’s and other dementias (ADRD), yet their capacity to prepare for hyper-complex climate-related disasters remains underexamined. Using geographic information systems (GIS), we mapped all licensed ALs with the Oregon Department of Forestry’s wildfire hazard scores, and then assessed organizational correlates of preparedness with a representative sample of Oregon ALs ( n = 321). ALs located in higher wildfire risk areas reported greater confidence in wildfire preparedness and were more likely to have received training and taken actions related to defensible space. However, communities serving residents with ADRD, as well as larger, nonprofit, and chain-affiliated ALs, expressed less confidence in engaging residents and implementing disaster protocols. These findings highlight important geographic and structural disparities in preparedness and underscore the need for tailored planning strategies that consider organizational characteristics and the increasing complexity of climate-related emergencies.

records.title: Multidimensional Losses and Mental Health of Older Adults in Puerto Rico in the Aftermath of Hurricane Mária
records.abstract: Natural disasters often deprive older adults of essential resources such as food, housing, and finances. Hurricane María devastated Puerto Rico in 2017. This study examines the types of losses experienced by older adults and the association of these losses with mental health 2 years later. We conducted face-to-face interviews with 154 older adults between 2019 and 2020 and found that two-thirds suffered home damage, and 47% lost food. We used latent class analysis to identify three typologies of loss: home damage, displacement, and multi-loss. Older adults who experienced home damage reported better mental health outcomes compared to those in the multi-loss group. Our findings suggest that the types and configurations of post-disaster loss can have different long-term effects on mental health, emphasizing the importance of addressing both essential basic needs and other forms of loss in disaster recovery efforts.

records.title: Age, Resilience, and Hope Predict Daily Functioning After a Flood
records.abstract: We examined associations among resilience characteristics, risk factors, and self-reported functional impairment using archival data from persons exposed to the 2016 flooding in Baton Rouge, LA. Three flood exposure groups were compared: non-flooded (controls), single disaster (flooded in 2016), and double disaster (flooded in 2005 and again in 2016). The Barkley Functional Impairment Scale (BFIS), a self-report measure of daily functioning, was the primary outcome measure. The single disaster group reported more problems in daily functioning than did the non-flooded controls. Correlations revealed that older age was associated with greater resilience and fewer risk characteristics. Regression analyses confirmed that age, resilience, and hope were associated with greater daily functioning after key sociodemographic factors and risk variables were accounted for. Strategies for managing the long-term impacts of multiple disasters for people who live in geographic areas that are prone to severe weather events are discussed.

records.title: Compound Disaster Exposure and Preparedness Among Older Adults: The Amplifying Role of Caregiving Responsibility
records.abstract: Older adults are especially vulnerable during disasters, yet the factors influencing their preparedness remain underexamined. This study investigates whether exposure to compound disasters (multiple, overlapping hazard events within a year) is associated with greater preparedness among older adults and whether caregiving responsibilities moderate this relationship. Using data from the 2022 and 2023 FEMA National Household Surveys ( N = 4,075), we employed multivariable logistic regression to assess the impact of compound exposure and its interaction with caregiving status on preparedness.  show that compound exposure increased the likelihood of being well-prepared, and caregiving responsibilities intensified this effect. These associations remained robust after controlling for demographic, socioeconomic, and psychosocial factors, including coping appraisal and information-seeking behavior. The findings suggest that caregiving may function as a motivator, enhancing protective action in high-risk contexts. Tailored preparedness initiatives that engage older caregivers may be critical for advancing disaster resilience in aging communities.

records.title: Evaluating Differences in Disaster-Related Staffing for Nursing Homes by Ownership Status
records.abstract: For-profit ownership has been linked to lower levels and skill composition of nursing home staffing, yet it is unclear whether disasters exacerbate these differences. We identified 914 nursing homes in Hurricane Ian’s path (September 2022), of which 665 (72.8%) were for-profit. We applied a comparative interrupted time series design to compare staffing hours per resident per day (HPRPD) before and after landfall. Before the storm, for-profit facilities staffed 9% fewer total HPRPD than not-for-profits (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.87–0.95), with similar deficits in the employed (permanent staff) (0.88, 95% CI 0.83–0.93) and licensed (0.90, 95% CI 0.86–0.94) categories. Both for-profit (1.04; 95% CI 1.03–1.05) and not-for-profit facilities (1.03; 95% CI 1.02–1.04) increased total staffing in the post-disaster period, driven by employed personnel; the difference in the magnitude of their responses (1%) was not statistically significant. Baseline staffing differences may affect nursing homes’ capacity to meet disaster-related needs.

records.title: The Impact of Hurricane Harvey on Home Health Care Delivery for Medicare Beneficiaries
records.abstract: Hurricanes can profoundly affect the delivery of home health (HH) services. We examined the impact of Hurricane Harvey on HH care in Texas, linking 2017-2018 patient-level Medicare HH claims with county-level data on disaster declarations from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. We used segmented interrupted time series to estimate monthly HH use changes among 142,416 beneficiaries in affected versus non-affected counties immediately after landfall (level change) and in its continued aftermath (trend change). HH nursing use dropped 16% immediately following hurricane and continued to decrease by 0-2%, statistically significant throughout post-Harvey period in the affected counties. However, similar impacts were also observed in non-affected counties. HH therapy use showed similar decreases, but with a smaller magnitude. Beneficiaries with the lowest function experienced significant larger immediate decreases in HH therapy use in the affected versus non-affected counties. Findings suggest the need to enhance mandatory disaster preparedness regulations in Medicare-certified HH agencies.

records.title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.

records.title: Implementing Dementia-Friendly Videos in Everyday Care: A Qualitative Study of Frontline Staff Experiences
records.abstract: Dementia-friendly videos are adapted audiovisual resources designed to support care for people living with moderate to severe dementia. Although evidence suggests these videos can enhance comfort, engagement, and communication, little is known about how frontline healthcare providers integrate them into everyday practice. This qualitative implementation study examined the barriers and facilitators experienced by frontline healthcare providers when implementing dementia-friendly videos in real-world clinical environments. The videos were introduced over an 18-month period in two contrasting care settings in Vancouver, Canada: an acute hospital geriatric unit and a long-term care dementia unit. Nineteen interdisciplinary healthcare providers, including nurses, care aides, and rehabilitation and recreation staff, participated in semi-structured interviews and focus groups after using the videos in routine care. A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted, followed by a later-stage comparison with relevant constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A participatory research team, including people living with dementia and family caregivers, contributed to study design, interpretation, and theme refinement. Findings showed that time pressures and staffing constraints limited workflow compatibility, particularly because many residents required assistance to operate devices. Limited equipment and unstable internet access further hindered consistent use. Facilitators included motivated staff who acted as catalysts for adoption, the perceived advantages of dementia-friendly videos over general platforms, and staff observations of positive impacts on emotional regulation and participation. Seeing benefits in practice, such as calming distressed patients, reinforced continued use. The study highlights the importance of integrating dementia-friendly videos into existing workflows rather than treating them as additional tasks. Ensuring adequate equipment, supporting motivated staff, and attending to cultural and linguistic relevance are essential for sustainable implementation. These findings offer practical guidance for embedding person-centred digital tools into dementia care.

records.title: Composition and size of close social networks among older adults in same-sex and different-sex couples
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study examines differences in the composition and size of the close social network among older adults in same-sex and different-sex coresidential unions.  Using pooled, probability-based, cross-sectional data from the 2006–2022 Health and Retirement Study, weighted fractional probit and negative binomial regression models were estimated to examine differences in close network composition (proportions of close children, immediate family members, and friends) and network size (number of close ties).  Compared with older adults in different-sex unions, those in same-sex unions reported a higher proportion of friends and a lower proportion of children and immediate family members in their close network, though overall network size was comparable. Supplemental analyses suggested heterogeneity in these patterns. The same-sex versus different-sex gap in friend composition was larger among males than females and was similarly larger among those who were cohabiting than married. Finally, in terms of network size, males in same-sex couples reported smaller close networks than males in different-sex couples, whereas network size was equivalent between females in same-sex and different-sex couples. Discussion Beyond their partners, older adults in same-sex unions cultivate distinctly friend-centered close networks. This pattern reflects a history of intentionally built chosen ties that queers dominant assumptions about who partnered older adults designate as close. These findings affirm the importance of policies and practices that acknowledge diverse family arrangements, particularly those rooted in chosen kinship, as a fundamental step toward achieving social equity.

records.title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal , we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.  In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences;  physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.  Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both  metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes. Discussion These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.

records.title: Caregiver Involvement in Dyadic Reminiscence Interventions for Persons With Dementia: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Reminiscence improves cognitive functions in persons with dementia (PWD) and strengthens familial relationships. However, the extent of dyadic reminiscence (caregivers’ involvement in delivering reminiscence), which impacts how interventions are designed for optimal home delivery, remains poorly mapped.  This scoping review mapped literature regarding dyadic home-based reminiscence interventions.  Six databases were searched for empirical studies. Two independent reviewers conducted screening and data extraction, followed by descriptive content analysis.  Thirty studies were included. Caregiver involvement formed a “continuum of engagement” across three broad categories: (i) observers of the PWD, (ii) co-creators of shared materials, and (iii) facilitators of reminiscence-based therapeutic strategies. Key outcomes included quality of life, dyadic relational experience, and PWD neuropsychiatric symptoms.  Caregivers should be recognised as active partners capable of shaping and enhancing intervention outcomes. Future research should prioritise exploring home-based reminiscence interventions that integrate caregiver participation as a core design element.

records.title: Continuing the Role: Lived Experiences of Family Caregivers after Placement of a Relative With Dementia in Residential Care
records.abstract: Placement of a relative with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) in residential care is often assumed to reduce caregiver burden. However, little is known about how informal caregivers experience their role after placement. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of 9 informal family caregivers whose relatives with ADRD resided in residential care settings. Semi-structured interviews lasting 60 to 120 minutes were conducted and analyzed using Colaizzi’s method to identify the essential structures of post-placement caregiving. Brief quantitative measures, including the CES-D-10 and the Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, were collected to contextualize participants’ emotional burden. Six themes emerged: emotional dissonance after placement, cognitive load and decision fatigue, persistence of caregiver identity and responsibility, fragmented systems and resource gaps, crisis-driven transitions, and the need for post-placement support. Participants described caregiving after placement not as an endpoint, but as a reconfigured role marked by ongoing emotional labor, vigilance, advocacy, and decision-making. Although physical caregiving tasks had shifted to staff, caregivers remained deeply involved in monitoring care quality, managing communication, responding to crises, and serving as the primary emotional anchor for their relatives. Quantitative findings reinforced these accounts, with all participants scoring above the CES-D-10 clinical threshold and reporting substantial caregiver distress. Taken together, the findings suggest that caregiving continues in sustained and multidimensional ways after residential placement. Residential care settings should recognize family caregivers as ongoing partners and provide structured orientation, clearer communication pathways, and psychosocial support to address the emotional, cognitive, and relational demands of post-placement caregiving.

records.title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
authors: Sabrina Simplício de Araújo Romero Ferrari
Bárbara Querem Hapuque da Silva Linhares
records.abstract: Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.

records.title: “Uncontrolled Hypertension Among Medicare Beneficiaries in Rural South Carolina.”
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: More than one-in-five older adults live in the rural U.S. Adults living in rural U.S. experience significantly higher hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular disease-related mortality compared to their urban counterparts. To extend the literature and provide real-world evidence, the primary  of this study was to estimate the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension and to identify factors associated with it among Medicare beneficiaries receiving care in rural South Carolina.  Data were used from the annual review of Abbeville County Medicare patients diagnosed with hypertension between July 2024 and January 2025. Uncontrolled hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg with or without antihypertensive medications. Generalized linear models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used to examine individual, behavioral, clinical, and area-level contextual factors associated with uncontrolled hypertension.  Responses from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension were analyzed: 55.6% females with a mean age (standard deviation) of 73.2±8.48 years. Overall, the prevalence (95% CI) of uncontrolled hypertension was 76.3% (95% CI: 73.2, 79.1). Compared with a healthy weight, being overweight (aOR=2.0; 95% CI: 1.2, 3.3; p = 0.005) or obese (aOR=2.1; 95% CI: 1.1, 2.8; p = 0.010) was associated with higher odds of uncontrolled hypertension. Contrary to previous findings, “most of the time” PA (aOR=1.57; 95% CI: 1.05-2.34; p = 0.027) was associated with a higher likelihood of uncontrolled hypertension compared to no PA.  Our findings highlight a high burden of uncontrolled hypertension in a rural Medicare population, underscore the need for  measures and further studies into the individual, behavioral, clinical, and contextual factors that may contribute to blood pressure control in rural communities.

records.title: Disability trajectories in the last years of life: a Swedish longitudinal multi-cohort study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: The patterns and determinants of late-life functional decline are not fully understood. We examined disability trajectories in relation to proximity to death among decedents aged 70 years and older, and investigated their associations with sex, age at death, education, cognitive impairment, and chronic conditions.  Harmonised data from six Swedish longitudinal ageing studies (1997–2016) within the National E-infrastructure for Aging Research (NEAR) were used. Participants who died at age 70 years or older and had data on activities of daily living (ADL) from at least two assessments were included (N = 2294, 62% women, mean age at death 89.8 years [SD 6.5]). ADL limitations (0–5 scale) were analysed across four time intervals before death (0–2, >2–4, >4–6, and 6–12 years). Group-based trajectory modelling identified disability trajectories, multinomial logistic regression examined demographic associations, and generalized estimating equations assessed associations of cognitive impairment and chronic conditions with trajectory membership.  Three trajectories were identified: constantly low (53%), low-sharply increasing (36%), and high-increasing (11%). Women, those with lower education, and individuals dying at older ages were more likely to follow increasing or persistently high disability trajectories. High-increasing trajectory was associated with higher likelihood of cognitive impairment.  For most, ADL limitations remained low until the final two years of life, though distinct trajectories with steady or sharp increases also emerged. Identifying demographic and health-related factors associated with functional decline may inform targeted interventions and help anticipate care needs.

records.title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation
records.abstract: Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.  This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.  We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired t tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.  Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen dz =0.28; P dz =0.40; P dz =0.42; P P =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638; P =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601; P =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111; P P P =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.  In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.

records.title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.  Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).  While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group. Discussion Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.

records.title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.  We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.  There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging. Discussion The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.

records.title: Older Adults share an agreement on experiences that elicit love: A study of consensus and individual differences in judgments
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Positive social connections are key ingredients for healthy aging. We studied older adults’ shared agreement on loving experiences and individual differences in their decisions-making to unlock critical information about how this developmental group connects socially.  To explore shared agreement on experiences of love, we surveyed a representative sample (N=400) of adults aged 65 years and older in the United States. They evaluated 61 experiences to determine whether older adults believe they typically evoke feelings of love in most people. We used a Bayesian decision tree model to account for individual differences in respondents’ knowledge and decision-making styles when deriving the consensus on these experiences.  We found a consensus among older adults on experiences of love. In addition, individual differences in knowledge on love and decision-making styles were meaningfully linked to person-level characteristics: female participants and those with higher levels of compassion had higher levels of knowledge on the consensus, White male participants and those with higher levels of loneliness were more likely to guess the shared agreement when they were uncertain, and non-White participants were more likely to guess “True.” Discussion Experiences of love for older adults include both romantic and non-romantic settings. Older adults tended to have different knowledge levels regarding the consensus on these experiences. Future research could examine whether fostering compassion or raising awareness about these loving experiences in daily life might improve well-being for older adults. Increased knowledge regarding these experiences may decrease misunderstandings or loneliness by sharing more loving experiences with others.

records.title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.  Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.  Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery. Discussion Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.

records.title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing. Method Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.  Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups. Discussion These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.

records.title: Statin use is associated with improved frailty trajectories in people with HIV
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Statins have pleiotropic properties beyond LDL cholesterol reduction, including anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects that may influence biological aging and frailty. The primary  was to compare frailty trajectories in people with HIV using statins for cardiovascular prevention with those not using statins. Secondary  included differences in walking speed, short physical performance battery, and hand grip strength. This observational longitudinal study included people with HIV from the Modena HIV Metabolic Clinic (Italy) with no prior statin use at baseline and at least three frailty index (FI) assessments. Baseline was the first visit with a FI assessment; follow-up was the last visit. Statin users and non-users were matched for follow-up duration. Time 0 (T0) was defined as statin initiation. Frailty was assessed with a 34-item FI. To minimize collider bias, lipid variables were excluded from the FI due to their direct relationship with statin exposure. Frailty trajectories and secondary outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed models. Beta-estimates were multiplied by 100 to improve readability. Among 3,444 people with HIV (69% men; median age 44.7 years), 23.1% initiated statins for primary prevention and 2.0% for secondary prevention. Statin users had a more unfavorable cardiometabolic profile at T0. In adjusted models, statin use was associated with a reduction in FI over time (statin*time interaction β=–2.562, 95%-CI –3.176,–1.987). No associations were observed with secondary outcomes. Statins may improve frailty trajectories, mitigate aging-related decline and preserve physical function in people with HIV, supporting a broader role for statins in HIV care.
