records.title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity
records.abstract: and  As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time. Research Design and  We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.  The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.  Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.

records.title: Care Choices Under the Shadow of Trauma: Childhood Trauma, Care Preparation, and Preferences in Later Life
records.abstract: Early-life experiences have a lasting impact on individual development and decision-making processes. Yet, the relationship between childhood trauma and care preferences in old age remains poorly understood.  This study aims to examine future care preferences from a life-course perspective, focusing on the mediating role of care preparation.  Data were used from the Panel Study of Ageing and Society (PAAS), comprising 5,007 participants aged 50 years and over in Hong Kong. Aging adults were first identified whether they have clear care preferences and then specified their preferences for formal and informal care.  Aging adults with greater exposure to childhood trauma are less likely to articulate care preferences. Among those who expressed care preferences, childhood trauma is associated with a higher likelihood of preferring formal care. The underlying pathways reveal that care preparation significantly mediated the associations between childhood trauma and care preferences.

records.title: Forecasting Assisted Living Facility Demand in Singapore: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average Projections
records.abstract: Singapore’s rapidly aging population presents significant challenges for healthcare planning and long-term care provision. This study applies ARIMA time-series modeling to forecast the number of older adults in assisted living facilities between 2025 and 2035. Using historical population data, nursing home residency figures, and simulated indicators of disability and living arrangements, the model projects assisted living demand rising from 19,741 individuals in 2025 to 29,443 in 2035—a 49.2% increase. While forecasts are conservative due to reliance on informal care from family members and foreign domestic helpers, structural shifts such as smaller family sizes and reduced caregiver availability may drive demand higher. The methodology highlights the importance of accounting for disability prevalence and informal care. Findings underscore the need for strategic planning to expand assisted living infrastructure, workforce capacity, and planning frameworks. Singapore’s case contributes to global literature by illustrating aging trajectories relevant to other developed societies.

records.title: Themes of Incongruence in the Relationships between Care Partners and Care Recipients During Discharge from Hospital to Home
records.abstract: and  Hospital-to-home transitions constitute vulnerable periods during which health systems increasingly rely on unpaid care partners to help care recipients execute discharge plans. We examine how mutuality and incongruence within care partner-care recipient dyads may shape discharge preparedness and dyadic self-efficacy during care transitions. Research Design and  We conducted a secondary qualitative analysis of PROJECT ACHIEVE focus groups and key informant interviews with 248 participants (138 care recipients, 110 care partners) across six U.S. health systems, examining their experiences of hospital-to-home transitions. A multidisciplinary team conducted thematic analysis and compared themes across stakeholder groups, guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Interdependence Theory.  Care recipients and care partners shared goals but often differed in their appraisals of discharge readiness and post-discharge roles. Three domains of incongruence emerged: (1) preparedness for transitions home, as care recipients prioritized going home despite ongoing symptoms while care partners worried about premature discharge and inadequate training; (2) burdensomeness and struggle for independence, as care recipients desired to preserve autonomy while care partners absorbed the emotional and practical strain of supporting such desires; and (3) role changes and evolving relational identities, as spouses and adult children assumed caregiving roles that disrupted prior identities in the relationship. Lower mutuality was linked to reduced dyadic self-efficacy and, consequently, increased risk of readmission.  Findings highlight dyadic incongruence as a target for intervention in care transitions. Care strategies that assess care recipient-care partner mutuality may enhance dyadic self-efficacy and improve post-discharge outcomes.

records.title: Evaluating the Implementation Fidelity of the REJOIN (Using Exercise to Relieve Joint Pain and Improve Aromatase Inhibitor Adherence in Older Breast Cancer Survivors) Pilot Trial
records.abstract: Implementation fidelity (IF), the extent to which interventions are delivered as intended, is essential for assessing program integrity and informing future dissemination/scalability. The REJOIN pilot trial adapted Fit & Strong! ( F&S! ) to deliver an education/exercise intervention targeting aromatase inhibitor-associated joint pain among older breast cancer survivors (BCS) at two institutions. An independent reviewer analyzed video-recorded sessions to assess IF domains (content, dose/exposure, delivery quality, participant responsiveness, contextual factors) using a 5-point Likert scale (1-low, 5-high). Overall, IF was high (mean 4.5/5.0), indicating successful implementation of the adapted F&S! curriculum. Content (mean = 4.4) showed minor curriculum deviations, dose/exposure (mean = 3.6) varied by session lengths, delivery quality (mean = 5.0) reflected enthusiastic ACSM and F&S! certified instructors, participant responsiveness (mean = 4.4) was evident through compliance/engagement, contextual factors (mean = 4.8) included additions of breast cancer specific content and adaptations and mitigating technical issues of remote delivery. Monitoring IF ensures program integrity and informs future intervention design/dissemination.

records.title: Intergenerational Queer Trajectories : Friendship and Connectedness among Younger and Older LGBTQ+ People in Ireland
records.abstract: This study examines intergenerational LGBTQ + friendships in Ireland, considering how queer understandings of time and ageing inform these relationships. Reflexive thematic analysis of life history interviews with seven younger (18-35) and seven older (60+) LGBTQ+ individuals revealed how shared queer experiences such as coming out, “gay age,” and relived adolescence create commonality and connection despite age differences. These friendships are also shaped through intergenerational exchange and “role modelling,” with LGBTQ+ knowledge and histories countering narratives like the “lonely old gay man” and offering alternative modes of queer ageing and living. While challenges arise from negative stereotypes, distinct historical contexts, and barriers to interaction, participants emphasise the sense of mutual understanding, historical connectedness, and hope for the future that underpins these bonds. Together, these findings illuminate what we term “intergenerational queer trajectories”: nonnormative life pathways involving shared queer experiences, histories, and imagined futures through which LGBTQ+ individuals connect across generations.

records.title: Navigating Leadership Challenges: Care Home Managers' and their Staffs’ Experiences of Enabling Person-Centred Dementia Care, A Qualitative Study
records.abstract: Care home managers’ leadership is widely recognised as shaping how staff provide care for people living with dementia. However, evidence remains limited on what enables managers to enact this role and sustain person-centred approaches within day-to-day care. This study explored managers and staffs’ experiences of facilitating person-centred care using an interpretative phenomenological approach. Twenty participants (ten managers and ten staff) from ten care homes took part in online semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using Colaizzi’s seven-step method. Participants viewed managers as key enablers of person-centred care, yet described this role as constrained and not always achievable in practice. Organisational and regulatory demands such as staffing shortages, administrative burden, and limited autonomy were perceived as major barriers, shaping what staff and managers felt able to prioritise. Managers countered these pressures, by being visible and available to staff, encouraging open communication, using staff meetings and appraisals to address concerns, and supporting staff reporting of poor practice. Values-based recruitment, emphasising empathy and kindness over formal qualifications, were also described as central to sustaining person-centred practice. However, staff were often unaware of these leadership strategies, which were frequently experienced as workarounds rather than embedded organisational processes. Examples of person-centred care focused on supporting residents’ choices in everyday routines and taking additional steps to understand individuals’ backgrounds when information was limited. Peer learning groups were valued for reducing managerial isolation and promoting shared problem-solving, whereas online and mandatory training were widely seen as insufficient. Findings highlight a persistent tension between managers and staff aspirations for person-centred care and the realities of practice shaped by system pressures, risk management, and resource constraints. Sustaining culture change requires long term organisational commitment, context sensitive leadership development, and structural support that extends beyond individual managers’ efforts.

records.title: Who Do You Trust? Demographic Patterns in Vaccine Hesitancy among Older Adults in a Rural State
records.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
records.abstract: Older adults are at increased risk for complications from vaccine-preventable diseases, yet many remain undervaccinated. This study examined demographic variability in vaccination hesitancy among older adults in a rural state and the potentially mediating role of trust uncertainty. A cross-sectional survey of a random sample of 739 adults aged 65+ in North Dakota was conducted from May to July 2022. Using bootstrapped mediation analyses, we assessed whether trust uncertainty mediated the relationships between demographic characteristics and vaccine hesitancy and acceptance.  showed uncertainty about whom to trust was a significant predictor of both higher vaccine hesitancy and lower vaccine acceptance. Uncertainty about whom to trust fully mediated the relationship between rurality and vaccine hesitancy, and between education and vaccine acceptance. Political leaning and physical health were also partially mediated through uncertainty about whom to trust. These findings highlight the role of trust in shaping vaccine attitudes and the need for tailored communication strategies that address information uncertainty.
